exports.name: AIPW
exports.docstring:
Augmented inverse-probability weighting (Stata ``teffects aipw``).

Combine the arm-specific outcome regressions with the weighting: the
regression supplies the prediction and the weights correct its residual::

    y_i(1) = yhat1_i + t_i (y_i - yhat1_i)/p_i
    y_i(0) = yhat0_i + (1-t_i)(y_i - yhat0_i)/(1-p_i)

The estimator is doubly robust -- either model may be misspecified without
destroying consistency -- which is why the reference value (2.018836) sits
between the regression-adjustment estimate (2.034515) and the pure weighting
estimate (1.888171).

Influence functions
-------------------
``theta = (beta, b1, b0)`` solves the stacked moments::

    m_i = [ x_i(t_i-p_i),  x_i t_i (y_i - x_i b1),  x_i (1-t_i)(y_i - x_i b0) ]

and the reported means add the augmented outcomes' own variation::

    psi_i = (a_i - A) + (dA/dtheta) psi_theta,i

Dropping the coefficient influence functions leaves 0.0641 against Stata's
0.0625084: the estimated components are negatively correlated with the
augmented outcome, so omitting them *inflates* the reported error.
exports.signature: (y: 'Any', treated: 'Any', x: 'Any', *, estimand: 'str' = 'ate') -> 'None'
exports.from_formula: (outcome: 'str', treatment: 'str', data: 'pd.DataFrame', **kwargs: 'Any') -> 'Any'
exports.fit: (self) -> 'TreatmentEffectResult'

exports.name: Areg
exports.docstring:
Linear regression absorbing categorical indicators -- Stata ``areg``.

This is a DIFFERENT command from ``reghdfe``, not a synonym, and the differences are
the reason it needs its own class:

==========================  ====================================================
``areg``                    ``reghdfe``
==========================  ====================================================
``absorb(varlist)`` REQUIRED, ``|`` block in the formula
banner "Linear regression, absorbing indicators"
``e(title2)`` = "Absorbed variable: firm"
``e(predict)`` = ``areg_p``  no predict program registered
``e(marginsnotok)`` = ``Residuals SCore D XBD``
==========================  ====================================================

All of those values come from ``tests/conformance/stata_fixtures/areg.json``, which is
a capture of the real command, not from reading prose.

The ESTIMATION is identical -- ``areg`` and ``reghdfe`` fit the same within model -- so
this subclass reuses :class:`FEOLS`'s machinery and overrides only the identity.

Parameters
----------
formula:
    ``"y ~ x1 + x2"`` alongside the ``absorb=`` keyword, matching Stata's
    ``areg y x1 x2, absorb(firm)``.  The ``|`` form is also accepted for symmetry with
    :class:`FEOLS`, but ``absorb=`` is the documented Stata spelling.
data:
    Estimation sample.
absorb:
    One or more categorical variables to absorb, e.g. ``"firm"`` or
    ``("firm", "year")``.  Required, as in Stata.

exports.name: ConsistencyError
exports.docstring:
Raised when a result cannot be guaranteed to be Stata-conformant.

This is deliberately loud: westata never silently returns a number that it
knows may diverge from Stata.  The message must say what diverged and which
evidence level the quantity has.

Also a ``ValueError`` for the same reason ``FormulaError`` is: the invalid input is a
value (too few clusters, a degenerate design) and callers legitimately write
``except ValueError``.  Adopting both bases lets a caller catch the specific class OR
the broad one, and -- more importantly -- lets ``except WestataError`` finally catch
the VCE refusals, which it did not.

Why that mattered: a single-cluster clustered VCE raised this from the logit path but
a plain ``ValueError`` from OLS/IV, so one library inconsistency produced two
different exception types for the same user error.  With both bases in place the sites
could be unified without breaking ``except ValueError``.

exports.name: Didregress
exports.docstring:
Two-way fixed-effects difference-in-differences (Stata ``didregress``).

Parameters
----------
outcome:
    Stata's first parenthesised block: the dependent variable, optionally
    followed by covariates -- ``"y"`` or ``"y x1 x2"``.  A sequence of
    names is accepted as well.
treatment:
    Stata's second block: exactly one treatment indicator.  It must be 0/1
    and vary within units; see the module docstring for the collinearity
    trap.
data:
    Estimation data in long (unit x period) form.
group:
    Column naming the unit whose fixed effect is absorbed and on which the
    standard errors are clustered.
time:
    Column naming the period whose fixed effect is absorbed.
covariates:
    Optional explicit covariate names, added to the tokens of ``outcome``.
    ``None`` (the default) adds no covariate, matching Stata's ``(y)``
    block.  Pass ``covariates="all"`` to use every remaining time-varying
    numeric column (the previous, opt-in behaviour) -- that path warns and
    reports the list through :attr:`inferred_covariates`.

Examples
--------
>>> result = Didregress.from_formula(              # doctest: +SKIP
...     "y x1", "treated", panel, group="unit", time="period"
... ).fit()
>>> float(result.params["treated"])                # the ATET
1.1861296209175862

exports.name: Eivreg
exports.docstring:
Errors-in-variables regression (Stata ``eivreg``).

``[R] eivreg`` Methods and formulas::

    A = X'X/n - S,   S = diag((1 - r_j) * s_j^2)
    b = A^-1 (X'y/n)

where ``r_j`` is the assumed reliability and ``s_j^2`` the *sample* variance
of that regressor (``1/n`` divisor -- Stata's own convention, and the reason
the cross-product must be normalised too).  The measurement-error variance
is subtracted from the cross-product, which undoes the attenuation rather
than reweighting: two plausible-looking reweightings by ``1/lambda`` and by
``lambda`` give x1 = 1.214 and 1.735 against Stata's 2.073214.

The variance is the M-estimator sandwich ``A^-1 (Psi'Psi/n) A^-1 / n`` with
the per-observation score

    psi_i = x_i u_i + sum_j (1 - r_j) (x_ij - xbar_j)^2 b_j e_j

The second term is the derivative of ``S`` with respect to ``b`` and is what
makes the standard errors move when a reliability is imposed; dropping it
leaves x1's standard error at .0965 against Stata's .0757645.

Fit statistics, all verified digit for digit::

    sigma^2 = (y'y - n b'Ab) / (n - k)          (Root MSE = .835714)
    R^2     = 1 - sigma^2 (n - k) / TSS         (0.8639837)
    F       = (b_s' V_ss^-1 b_s) / (k - 1)      (407.77933)
exports.signature: (endog: 'Any', exog: 'Any', reliab: 'Mapping[str, float]', *, param_names: 'Sequence[str]', model_data: 'pd.DataFrame | None' = None) -> 'None'

exports.name: Etregress
exports.docstring:
Endogenous treatment regression (Stata ``etregress``), control function.

Treatment equation (probit, full sample)::

    t* = z g + u,   t = 1[t* > 0]

Outcome equation (full sample, unlike :class:`Heckman`)::

    y = x b + d t + e

The control function adds the first-stage residual
``t*phi(z g)/Phi(z g) - (1-t)*phi(z g)/(1-Phi(z g))`` to the outcome
regression, which absorbs the correlation between ``u`` and ``e`` and makes
the treatment coefficient ``d`` consistent.

Parameters
----------
formula:
    ``"y ~ x + treat(t ~ z)"``.  The treatment indicator is added to the
    outcome equation automatically; naming it there as well
    (``"y ~ x + t + treat(t ~ z)"``) is accepted and does not duplicate it.

Notes
-----
``y`` is observed for treated and control units alike, so every row enters
the outcome equation -- that is the structural difference from
:class:`Heckman`, where the outcome is truncated by selection.

Standard errors are the two-step M-estimator sandwich (see the module
docstring), not naive OLS standard errors and not Stata's ML ones.
exports.signature: (outcome: 'np.ndarray', outcome_exog: 'np.ndarray', treatment: 'np.ndarray', treatment_exog: 'np.ndarray', *, outcome_names: 'Sequence[str]', treatment_names: 'Sequence[str]', treated: 'np.ndarray', model_data: 'pd.DataFrame | None' = None) -> 'None'

exports.name: FormulaError
exports.docstring:
Raised when a model formula cannot be evaluated on the given data.

This deliberately wraps ``patsy.PatsyError``.  Patsy evaluates formulas
through its own namespace object held in the traceback frame, and a raw
``PatsyError`` therefore keeps that frame alive; several exception
formatters (including pytest's) then fail while introspecting it and the
user sees an internal rendering error instead of the actual message.
Re-raising a plain exception with the original text keeps the diagnostic.

exports.name: GARCH
exports.docstring:
GARCH / EGARCH volatility model (Stata ``arch``).

Parameters
----------
endog:
    Returns series.
p, q:
    ARCH and GARCH orders.
o:
    Asymmetry order (``o=1`` gives GJR-GARCH).
vol:
    ``"GARCH"`` or ``"EGARCH"``.
dist:
    Innovation distribution: ``"normal"`` or ``"t"``.
mean:
    Mean equation; ``"Constant"`` matches Stata's default ``arch ...,
    arch(1) garch(1)``.

Notes
-----
Two of ``arch`` the package's defaults are NOT Stata's, and both are
overridden here because they change reported numbers:

*standard errors*  Stata's ``arch`` reports ``e(vcetype) = "OPG"`` (BHHH:
``inv(sum_t s_t s_t')``).  The package's default is ``cov_type="robust"``
(Bollerslev-Wooldridge).  On the 600-observation reference series the two
differ by up to 52% on a standard error, so ``fit(cov_type="opg")`` is the
default here.

*presample variance*  The GARCH recursion needs ``h_0``.  Stata uses
``e(archi) = mean(demeaned residual^2)``; the package uses an exponentially
weighted backcast (``0.94**j`` weights over the first 75 residuals).  The
two imply slightly different objective functions, so the maximisers differ
(mu by 1.1e-2 relative).  ``fit(presample="stata")`` iterates the Stata
convention to a fixed point, which brings all four parameters within 1.8e-4
of Stata's.

Neither of these makes the estimates identical to Stata's, and the reason is
documented rather than absorbed.  The remaining residual is **~1.8e-4
relative in the parameters and ~1.5e-4 in the standard errors** (measured on
the reference GARCH(1,1) series against StataNow 19.5).  It is NOT a formula
difference:

* evaluating Stata's own variance recursion at STATA's reported parameters
  gives ``ll = -824.3780305032``, while Stata *reports*
  ``e(ll) = -824.3779300106`` -- i.e. Stata's printed likelihood sits
  **1.00e-04 above** what its own recursion yields at its own estimates, so
  Stata's first-observation (``e(condobs) = 0``) handling is slightly
  different from the plain recursion;
* evaluating the same recursion at westata's estimates gives
  ``-824.3780321``, only **1.6e-06** from Stata's recursion at Stata's
  estimates.

So both sides sit at essentially the same optimum of the same objective, and
the gap is Stata's stopping point plus that 1e-4 accounting difference.  A
1e-9 match would require reproducing Stata's exact conditional-observation
terms; see ``retest/fix/tseries/repro_v6_arch.py`` for the full
decomposition and ``retest/fix/tseries/FIXES.md`` for the residual table.

exports.name: Heckman
exports.docstring:
Heckman sample-selection model (Stata ``heckman``), two-step estimator.

Selection equation (probit, full sample)::

    s* = z g + u,   s = 1[s* > 0]

Outcome equation (observed only where ``s == 1``)::

    y = x b + e

Step 1 estimates ``g`` and forms the inverse Mills ratio
``lambda = phi(z g)/Phi(z g)``; step 2 regresses ``y`` on ``x`` and
``lambda`` over the selected rows.

Parameters
----------
formula:
    ``"y ~ x + select(s ~ z)"``.  The selection indicator must be 0/1 and
    the selection equation is estimated on the full sample, which is the
    point of the estimator: a missing ``y`` is what marks a non-selected
    observation, so ``y`` may be missing off the selected rows.

Notes
-----
Standard errors are the two-step M-estimator sandwich: the first stage's
estimation error is propagated into the second stage, so they are *not*
naive OLS standard errors (see the module docstring).  They are also not
Stata's ML standard errors, because these are two-step estimates.
exports.signature: (outcome: 'np.ndarray', outcome_exog: 'np.ndarray', selection: 'np.ndarray', selection_exog: 'np.ndarray', *, outcome_names: 'Sequence[str]', selection_names: 'Sequence[str]', selected: 'np.ndarray', model_data: 'pd.DataFrame | None' = None) -> 'None'

exports.name: IPW
exports.docstring:
Inverse-probability weighting (Stata ``teffects ipw``).

Fit a logit treatment model and reweight outcomes by the inverse propensity
score.  Stata reports the **normalised** (Hajek) weighted means::

    ATE  = mean(t*y/p)/mean(t/p) - mean((1-t)*y/(1-p))/mean((1-t)/(1-p))
    ATET = mean(t*y)/mean(t)     - mean((1-t)*y*odds)/mean((1-t)*odds)

with ``odds = p/(1-p)``.  The normalisation is not cosmetic: the
unnormalised sums give 1.9355 on the reference data where Stata gives
1.8882, because the estimated propensities do not add up to the arm sizes
exactly.  The ATET reweights the controls to the treated propensity
distribution through the odds, which is why its control mean (1.5641) sits
above the ATE's (1.0182).

Influence functions
-------------------
The estimator is an M-estimator with ``theta = (beta, mu1, mu0)`` solving
``mean(m_i) = 0`` for::

    m_i = [ x_i (t_i - p_i),  t_i (y_i - mu1)/p_i,  (1-t_i)(y_i-mu0)/(1-p_i) ]

so the ATE standard error comes from the full sandwich.  Treating the
propensity score as fixed instead reports 0.1216 for ``POmean(0)`` against
Stata's 0.1001317, because the treatment-model error is then ignored.
exports.signature: (y: 'Any', treated: 'Any', x: 'Any', *, estimand: 'str' = 'ate') -> 'None'
exports.from_formula: (outcome: 'str', treatment: 'str', data: 'pd.DataFrame', **kwargs: 'Any') -> 'Any'

exports.name: IVGMM
exports.docstring:
Generalized method of moments (Stata ``ivregress gmm``).

``ivregress gmm`` has *two* choices tied to ``vce()``, not one:

* the covariance of ``e(b)`` (as for every IV estimator), and
* the GMM weight matrix ``W``, which ``ivregress`` sets from the same
  moment covariance the ``vce()`` implies.

So ``ivregress gmm, vce(cluster gid)`` clusters ``W`` too, and the *point
estimates* move (3.58e-2 on the 140x14 panel of the retest).  westata
therefore picks the backend weight matrix from ``cov_type``: the default
heteroskedastic ("robust") one, or ``weight_type="clustered"`` when
``cov_type="cluster"``.  Verified against StataNow 19.5: coefficients and
``e(V)`` both agree to <= 5e-14 (140x14 and 240x24 panels, 2 and 3
instruments).

The covariance is the GMM weight-matrix sandwich from the backend; it
cannot be expressed through :func:`westata.vce.dispatch.compute_cov`, which
assumes an OLS-shaped bread.

exports.name: Logit
exports.docstring:
Logistic regression (Stata ``logit``).

NO INTERCEPT IS ADDED. The design matrix passed to ``Logit(y, X, ...)`` is taken as COMPLETE,
exactly as statsmodels treats it. Stata's ``logit y x1 x2`` adds a constant for you, so the two
calls are not equivalent:

    ws.Logit(y, X, param_names=["x1", "x2"])            # no constant -> different model
    ws.Logit.from_formula("y ~ x1 + x2", frame)         # constant included, matches Stata

Getting this wrong does not raise: it returns a well-formed fit with plausible coefficients
that disagree with Stata, which reads as a numerical defect rather than a missing column.
Measured on grilic.dta with a median split of lnw:

    array interface, no constant   coef [.002219, -.000498, .052896]
    Stata `logit hi s expr tenure`  coef [.459083, .158881, .153049], _cons -6.691539

To keep the array interface and still match Stata, pass a column of ones yourself:

    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(frame)), frame[["s", "expr", "tenure"]]])
    ws.Logit(y, X, param_names=["_cons", "s", "expr", "tenure"])

       0     0      0    | .00001555 -1.3655805 1.1794885 | ...

exports.name: Mvreg
exports.docstring:
Multivariate regression (Stata ``mvreg``).

Every equation shares one design matrix, so the coefficients are exactly
per-equation OLS; only the VCE uses the cross-equation residual covariance::

    V = Sigma (x) (X'X)^-1,    Sigma_ij = u_i'u_j / (n - k)

Note the ``n - k`` here, against ``n`` for ``sureg``: ``mvreg`` is a
multivariate least-squares problem with a common design, and Stata's
standard errors only reproduce with the degrees-of-freedom divisor.

``mvreg`` and ``sureg`` therefore disagree on identical data whenever the
equations contain different regressors -- ``mvreg`` puts every regressor in
every equation.  That is a specification difference, not an inconsistency.

exports.from_formula: (formula: 'str', data: 'pd.DataFrame', *, subset: 'Any' = None) -> "'Mvreg'"

exports.name: NearestNeighbourMatching
exports.docstring:
Nearest-neighbour matching (Stata ``teffects nnmatch``).

Impute each observation's counterfactual from the ``nneighbor`` closest
observations in the other arm, measured by the **Mahalanobis** distance
under the sample covariance of the covariates -- which is what
``teffects nnmatch`` uses by default and what reproduces its 2.051839
exactly on the reference data.  Euclidean distance gives 2.046771, about
0.25% away, so the metric is not a detail.  Matching is with replacement, so
a control may serve several treated units.

Standard errors: an approximation, and labelled as one
------------------------------------------------------
``se_method`` on the result reads ``"Abadie-Imbens approximation"`` rather
than ``"influence function"``, because this is the one estimator here whose
variance is **not** reproduced exactly.  Stata reports 0.0691114 for the
fixture; the implementation below gives 0.0706220, a gap of +2.2%.

The gap lives entirely in the estimated conditional variance
``sigma^2(X_i)``.  The Abadie-Imbens variance has the form

    V = (1/n^2) sum_i (1 + K_i)^2 sigma^2_i

where ``K_i`` counts how often observation ``i`` is reused as a match -- the
reuse term is the whole point, since a control used many times injects its
noise many times.  ``K_i`` is reproduced exactly; ``sigma^2_i`` is estimated
here as ``0.5 (y_i - y_j)^2`` with ``j`` the nearest **same-arm** neighbour,
which is the standard matching estimator of the conditional variance.
Several plausible variants bracket Stata's number (0.0691 to 0.0706) without
singling out one, and Stata's exact estimator for this term is not publicly
documented to the digit, so the honest move is to report the measured gap
rather than tune a constant until one sample lines up.

Because the ATE variance is asymptotic for the effect, the potential-outcome
means have no separate matching variance; their reported standard errors are
the effect's error rescaled by the share of the sample each mean covers, and
they inherit the same caveat.
exports.signature: (y: 'Any', treated: 'Any', x: 'Any', *, nneighbor: 'int' = 1, estimand: 'str' = 'ate') -> 'None'
exports.from_formula: (outcome: 'str', treatment: 'str', data: 'pd.DataFrame', **kwargs: 'Any') -> 'Any'
exports.fit: (self) -> 'TreatmentEffectResult'

Negative binomial regression (Stata ``nbreg``).

statsmodels parameterises the dispersion as ``alpha`` (``Var = mu +
alpha*mu^2``), the same as Stata's default ``nbreg`` output.  ``bfgs`` is
used rather than Newton: the alpha parameter makes the Newton step diverge
when started from the Poisson fit, which is statsmodels' own
``NegativeBinomial.fit`` default for this reason.

exports.name: NegativeBinomialNB1
exports.docstring:
Negative binomial regression with a CONSTANT dispersion (Stata ``nbreg, dispersion(constant)``).

NB1 has ``Var = mu (1 + delta)``, so the variance is linear in the mean; Stata's default NB2 has
``Var = mu + alpha mu^2``. They are different models with different likelihoods, which is why this is a
separate class rather than a flag on :class:`NegativeBinomial`.

The likelihood and score are transcribed from ``nbreg_al.ado`` (lines 19-52), including the
parameterisation that is easy to miss: the gamma terms involve

    m = exp(xb - lndelta) = mu / delta

not ``mu``. Using ``mu`` there still converges and reports plausible coefficients -- it just fits a
different model, and the mismatch only shows up when the likelihood is compared at STAT'S estimates.

Verified on the sweep's own data against a live Stata: coefficients 5.8e-10, ``delta`` 6.0e-10,
log-likelihood 2.3e-14.

exports.name: Newey
exports.docstring:
``newey depvar indepvars, lag(#)`` -- OLS with a HAC (Newey-West) VCE.

The class form of :func:`westata.newey`, provided so that an estimation command can
be used the same way as every other one in the package::

    ws.Newey.from_formula("y ~ x1 + x2", data, lag=1).fit()
    ws.newey("y ~ x1 + x2", data, lag=1)      # the same fit, still supported

Why this is a class at all (R2.7): ``newey`` is an ESTIMATION command -- it consumes
raw data -- not a post-estimation command.  Before this, it was one of 19 estimation
commands reachable only as a bare function, so the same operation had a construction
step in some families (``ws.OLS.from_formula(...).fit()``) and none in others.  The
function remains as a thin wrapper; there is exactly one implementation.

``lag`` is REQUIRED and belongs to the model, not to ``fit()``: it selects the
estimator (how many autocovariances enter the HAC sum), and Stata declares it a
required option with no default (``newey.ado:15``, ``newey.sthlp:55``).

``fit()`` takes NO ``cov_type``.  That is deliberate, not an oversight: Stata's
``newey`` has no ``vce()`` option at all -- the HAC variance IS the estimator -- so
accepting one here would be an interface that promises a choice that does not exist
(R2.1, R1.5).

Two things differ from a plain ``StataResults`` and both are visible to
callers, so they cannot be left to inheritance:

* ``e()`` holds only ``newey``'s scalars (managed by :func:`newey`);
* ``predict`` accepts only ``xb``/``index``/``stdp``/``residuals``

exports.name: PanelOLS
exports.docstring:
Fixed-effects panel regression (Stata ``xtreg, fe``).

Parameters
----------
formula:
    Two-sided formula in statsmodels/patsy syntax, for example
    ``"y ~ x1 + x2"``.  The constant is implied by patsy exactly as in
    :class:`westata.estimators.linear.OLS`, so ``e(b)`` includes
    ``Intercept`` even though the within transformation absorbs it.
    Drop it with ``"y ~ x1 + x2 - 1"`` to follow Stata's ``noconstant``.
data:
    Panel frame.  Either a long frame with the ``entity``/``time`` columns,
    or a frame already indexed by a two-level ``(entity, time)``
    ``MultiIndex`` (``entity``/``time`` must then name two of its levels).
entity, time:
    Names of the panel dimensions.

Notes
-----
Rows with missing values are dropped listwise *before* estimation, and the
retained sample is what ``e(N)`` counts, so ``e(N)`` can be smaller than
``len(data)`` - the same behaviour as Stata's ``regress``/``xtreg``.

Known deviations: ``e(df_m)``, ``e(rank)`` and ``e(df_b)`` under clustering
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Deliberate, and approved by the Lead.  Stata's own ``e()`` block disagrees
with itself here, so westata does not copy it.

Measured with StataNow 19.5 on 2026-10-24, 30 entities x 6 periods,
``xtset id t``::

    command                                  e(df_m) e(df_b) e(rank)  prints
    xtreg y x1,     fe vce(cluster id)          0      1       1      F(1, 29) = 211.29
    xtreg y x1 x2,  fe vce(cluster id)          1      2       2      F(2, 29) = 303.80
    xtreg y x1 x2 z, fe vce(cluster id)         2      3       3      F(3, 29) = 254.47

Stata's clustered ``xtreg, fe`` redefines both scalars relative to the
*reported* model, not to the parameter vector:

* ``e(df_m) = slopes - 1`` (the reported rank minus one),
* ``e(rank)  = slopes``,

while the F it prints and the ``e(p)`` it stores are
``F(e(df_b), e(df_r))``.  With two slopes, ``e(df_m)`` says 1, ``e(rank)``
says 2, and the printed test is ``F(2, 29)``.  Stata also keeps the
unclustered values in ``e(df_r_mb) = 148`` and ``e(rank_mb) = 3``, which is
what shows the redefinition is deliberate: under clustering both scalars
shift down by one because Stata counts the *free* parameters of the
clustered problem (the slopes alone) rather than the model's columns.

westata reports the parameter vector's own quantities - ``e(df_m)`` = the
number of slopes (2), ``e(rank)`` = ``len(e(b))`` = slopes + 1 (3, the
constant included) - plus ``e(df_b)`` = 2.  So against Stata's clustered
values, ``e(df_m)`` is +1 and ``e(rank)`` is +1:

=====================  =========  =========  =======
quantity               Stata      westata    delta
=====================  =========  =========  =======
``e(df_m)`` (2 slopes)       1          2      +1
``e(rank)``  (2 slopes)      2          3      +1
``e(df_b)``                  2          2       0
``e(df_r)``                 29         29       0
``e(F)``                 303.80     303.80       0  (6.5e-16 relative)
=====================  =========  =========  =======

Copying Stata's ``e(df_m)`` would make the summary read ``F(1, 29) = 303.80``
- a degrees-of-freedom label contradicting its own p-value - so a visibly
wrong *label* is the lesser evil than a wrong *number*.  ``e(rank)`` is kept
as the honest rank of the fitted model for the same class of reason: it is
what :class:`westata.results.StataResults` and the postestimation machinery
use for the size of ``e(b)``/``e(V)``, and shrinking it to Stata's
clustered-scalar convention would silently change unrelated scalars
(``aic``/``bic``-style counts, ``/sigma`` handling) that read it.  Changing
either number is therefore out of scope for a documentation fix; only the
F statistic has to match, and it does.

The real fix, if the Lead ever wants bit-for-bit ``e()`` equality, is to
store Stata's values and teach :mod:`westata.results.summary` to label F
tests from ``e(df_b)`` - that needs a file outside this module's ownership.

Everything else about a clustered ``xtreg, fe`` is reproduced, including
``e(df_r) = G - 1`` (``29`` on that panel, with the model-based ``148`` in
``e(df_r_mb)``) and the ``N - rank`` denominator Stata uses for
``e(rmse)``/``e(r2_a)`` under clustering.

The class form of :func:`westata.prais`, so an estimation command can be used the same
way as every other one in the package (R2.7)::

    ws.Prais.from_formula("y ~ x", data).fit()
    ws.Prais(data, "y ~ x").fit()          # same construction, function order kept
    ws.prais(data, "y ~ x")                # the documented function, still supported

NOTE THE POSITIONAL ORDER.  ``Prais(data, formula)`` keeps the FUNCTION's order, which
is the reverse of every ``from_formula`` in the package.  That is deliberate: 52 call
sites pass ``ws.prais(frame, FORMULA)`` positionally, and swapping the two would not
raise -- ``data`` and ``formula`` are both positional, so a swapped call would try to
parse the frame as a formula and fail with an error that names neither.  Use
:meth:`from_formula` for the standard ``(formula, data)`` order.

``fit()`` takes NO ``cov_type``: Stata's ``prais`` has no ``vce()`` option, and the
AR(1)-transformed least squares is the estimator itself (R2.1, R1.5).

         3 vs 2  |   .0148523   .0193778     -.0249792    .0546839

exports.name: RandomEffectsMLE
exports.docstring:
Random-effects by MAXIMUM LIKELIHOOD (Stata ``xtreg, mle``).

``xtreg, re`` is a GLS estimator that plugs in Swamy-Arora variance components;
``xtreg, mle`` maximises the same random-effects likelihood over the coefficients AND the
two variance components at once. They are different estimators and give different numbers:

    re   ltlan .565591486884  ltwlab .144184445858  sigma_u .133248446685
    mle  ltlan .564328798388  ltwlab .140897433220  sigma_u .214109360143

``sigma_u`` differs by 60%, so this cannot be emulated by adjusting the GLS output.

Fitted with statsmodels' ``MixedLM`` (ML, not REML -- Stata's ``xtreg, mle`` maximises the
full likelihood). Nelder-Mead is used rather than the default because it lands closer to
Stata's optimum on the reference fit: llf 332.8973943565 against 332.8973943543, with
``ltlan`` agreeing to 1.6e-7 where the default was 9.8e-7 away.

Standard errors come from the inverse of the observed information, which is what Stata
reports; the reference values agree to about 1e-6.
exports.signature: (formula: 'str', data: 'pd.DataFrame', *, entity: 'str', time: 'str', weights: 'Any' = None, weight_type: 'str | None' = None) -> 'None'

exports.name: RdRobustResult
exports.docstring:
``rdrobust``: sharp RD estimate at a cutoff.

``se``/``z``/``pvalue``/``ci`` are ``nan`` when the variance estimator could not be
reproduced; ``variance_matches_stata`` records which case applies.

WHY THE VARIANCE IS NOT REPRODUCED -- and this one IS a hard boundary, unlike several
earlier gaps in this codebase that turned out to be recoverable. The point estimate
matches Stata exactly (``rdrobust diff border, c(30) h(5) b(8)`` gives tau_cl
121.297562295 here and 121.297562295 in Stata). The variance is computed inside
``rdrobust_vce``, which lives ONLY in the compiled Mata library
``~/ado/plus/l/lrdrobust.mlib`` -- there is no ``.ado``/``.mata`` source for it, unlike
``rdrobust.ado`` itself, which IS readable at ``~/ado/plus/r/rdrobust.ado`` (1331 lines).

What the readable part pins down, verified against Stata's own ``e(V_cl_l)`` /
``e(V_cl_r)`` (h(5) b(8) on border.dta, cutoff 30)::

    V_cl_l = [[496.94559, 225.18263], [225.18263, 167.66193]]
    V_cl_r = [[4303.6294, -1188.4335], [-1188.4335, 336.15059]]
    sqrt((V_cl_l + V_cl_r)[1,1]) = 69.2861818   == Stata se_tau_cl 69.2861819408

i.e. ``se = sqrt((V_l + V_r)[deriv, deriv])`` in zero-based terms -- the Mata code's
``[deriv+1, deriv+1]``. What is NOT recovered is how V_l/V_r are built from the
residuals. The standard CR1 sandwich candidates were tried and all miss on the very
section used for the check above (n_left = 5, only a 2-column design):

    w^2 * res^2   ->  38.16     (target 496.95)
    w   * res^2   -> 240.47
    w   * res^2 * n -> 1202.33

Reporting any of those would be the plausible-but-wrong number this project refuses, so
the inferential fields stay NaN and the test suite asserts that they do.
exports.signature: (tau: 'float', cutoff: 'float', bandwidth: 'float', bias_bandwidth: 'float', nobs: 'int', nobs_left: 'int', nobs_right: 'int', nobs_effective_left: 'int', nobs_effective_right: 'int', order: 'int', bias_order: 'int', kernel: 'str', coef_covs: 'Any' = None, se: 'float' = nan, z: 'float' = nan, pvalue: 'float' = nan, ci_lower: 'float' = nan, ci_upper: 'float' = nan, variance_matches_stata: 'bool' = False) -> None

exports.name: RegressionAdjustment
exports.docstring:
Regression adjustment (Stata ``teffects ra``).

Fit the outcome model ``y ~ x`` **separately** in each treatment arm, predict
both potential outcomes for every observation, and average::

    yhat1 = X @ b1       ATE  = mean(yhat1 - yhat0)
    yhat0 = X @ b0       ATET = mean over the treated of (yhat1 - yhat0)

with ``POmean(0) = mean(yhat0)`` and ``POmean(1) = mean(yhat1)`` (taken over
the treated for the ATET).  Allowing the slopes to differ by arm is what
separates this from a single regression with a treatment dummy, and on the
reference data it is the difference between 2.0345 and a badly biased number.

Influence functions
-------------------
Two sources of sampling error matter, and the second is the one that is easy
to forget.  The residuals ``y - yhat`` are orthogonal to the design within
each arm, so the usual score terms vanish identically; what remains is the
error in the estimated *coefficients*::

    psi_i = (yhat1_i - yhat0_i) - ATE + (u1_i - u0_i)' xbar

where ``u_t,i = (X_t'X_t / n)^{-1} x_i t_i e_i`` is the coefficient influence
function of arm ``t``.  Dropping that term reports 0.0018 instead of Stata's
0.0610149 -- a 33-fold understatement that no point-estimate test would
notice.  For the ATET the leading term is divided by ``mean(t)`` and the
coefficient influence is evaluated at the treated covariate mean.
exports.signature: (y: 'Any', treated: 'Any', x: 'Any', *, estimand: 'str' = 'ate') -> 'None'
exports.from_formula: (outcome: 'str', treatment: 'str', data: 'pd.DataFrame', **kwargs: 'Any') -> 'Any'

exports.name: SvyLogit
exports.docstring:
Survey-weighted logistic regression (``svy: logit``).

Pseudo-maximum-likelihood with sampling weights, linearised with
``psi_i = I^-1 w_i x_i (y_i - p_i)`` where ``I = X' diag(w p(1-p)) X``.

Conformance note
----------------
On the fixture design the estimates reproduce Stata to about ``5e-10``
relative.  That residual is **Stata's stopping tolerance, not this code's**:
evaluating Stata's own score equations at Stata's published coefficients
leaves a gradient of ``1.7e-8``, while the estimates returned here are the
exact maximiser (gradient ``8e-15``).  A conformance tolerance tighter than
``1e-9`` would therefore assert something untrue about Stata rather than
about westata.

part of the linearisation; see the module docstring and
``test_mean_requires_the_weight_inside_the_influence``.

exports.name: Truncreg
exports.docstring:
Truncated regression (Stata ``truncreg``).

Observations outside ``(lower, upper)`` are absent from the sample, so each
contribution is the normal density divided by the probability of falling
inside the interval.

Parameters
----------
endog:
    Observed outcome; every value must lie strictly inside the limits.
exog:
    Design matrix including a constant.
lower, upper:
    Truncation limits in the units of ``endog``; at least one is required.
    Use ``None`` for an open limit (``-inf`` / ``+inf``).

Notes
-----
Stata's ``truncreg`` excludes observations with ``y <= lower`` or
``y >= upper`` from the estimation sample and reports the count as
``(N obs truncated)``; this does the same, records the count in
``e(n_truncated)`` and warns, because silently changing the sample would
make ``e(N)`` impossible to reconcile with the input data.
exports.signature: (endog: 'Any', exog: 'Any', *, lower: 'float | None' = None, upper: 'float | None' = None, param_names: 'list[str] | None' = None) -> 'None'

exports.docstring:
Wrapper over a fitted VAR with Stata-flavoured accessors.

Stata's ``var`` normalises the residual covariance by **T per equation**,
not by ``T - k_eq`` where ``k_eq`` is that equation's regressor count.  The
two differ by the factor ``(T - k_eq)/T`` -- 0.98997 for a bivariate VAR(1)
on 299 usable observations (``k_eq = 3``) -- which is exactly the gap the
retest measured on ``bse``, ``e(Sigma)`` and ``vargranger``.  Every
Stata-facing accessor here applies that factor; ``raw_result`` remains
available for the statsmodels convention.

exports.name: XtGls
exports.docstring:
Panel GLS (Stata ``xtgls``) with a Kronecker error structure.

``[XT] xtgls`` Methods and formulas defines ``Omega = Sigma_{m x m} kron
I_{T_i x T_i}`` with ``Sigma_ij = e_i'e_j / T`` estimated from **OLS**
residuals, and the estimator as

.. math:: \hat\beta = (X'\hat\Omega^{-1} X)^{-1} X'\hat\Omega^{-1} y,
          \qquad V(\hat\beta) = (X'\hat\Omega^{-1} X)^{-1}.

This is a *two-step* FGLS, not OLS: the panel-specific variances reweight each
panel, so the coefficients move whenever those variances are correlated with
the regressors.  The P9 plan asserts that ``panels(heteroskedastic)`` "must
equal pooled OLS exactly"; that holds only when all panels share one residual
variance.  On the fixture data OLS gives x1 = .7533126 and Stata's ``xtgls``
gives .6798471.  westata follows Stata and the manual, and the test file pins
the OLS identity on a homoskedastic panel where it really does hold.

``panels(iid)``, ``panels(heteroskedastic)`` and ``panels(correlated)`` are
implemented.  ``corr(ar1)``/``corr(psar1)`` and ``igls`` raise
:class:`westata.errors.UnsupportedError`: they change the estimator, not a
display option, so a "nearby" answer would be wrong in a way the user could
not see.
exports.signature: (endog: 'Any', exog: 'Any', codes: 'np.ndarray', sizes: 'np.ndarray', *, param_names: 'Sequence[str]', panels: 'str' = 'heteroskedastic', corr: 'str' = 'independent', nmk: 'bool' = False, model_data: 'pd.DataFrame | None' = None) -> 'None'
exports.from_formula: (formula: 'str', data: 'pd.DataFrame', *, entity: 'str', time: 'str | None' = None, panels: 'str' = 'heteroskedastic', corr: 'str' = 'independent', nmk: 'bool' = False, subset: 'Any' = None) -> "'XtGls'"

exports.name: XtIvreg
exports.docstring:
Panel instrumental variables (Stata ``xtivreg``), ``fe`` and ``re``.

``fe`` (within 2SLS)
    The within transform is applied to the dependent variable, the exogenous
    regressors, the endogenous regressors **and the instruments**.  The last
    one is the trap: an instrument that is not demeaned still carries the
    entity effect, so the projection would re-absorb part of the fixed effect
    the transform was meant to remove.  Stata then reports the conventional
    VCE rescaled by ``(N - K) / (N - n - K + 1)`` -- the ``n - 1`` estimated
    means correction (``[XT] xtivreg`` Methods and formulas).  The within
    transform removes the constant, so ``_cons`` is recovered afterwards from
    the entity means, ``ybar - xbar'b``.

``re`` (G2SLS)
    Swamy-Arora variance components give
    ``theta = 1 - sqrt(sigma_e^2 / (T sigma_u^2 + sigma_e^2))``; everything,
    again including the instruments, is quasi-demeaned before 2SLS.  The
    conventional VCE is ``e'e/(N-K)`` on the transformed regression.

Formula syntax
--------------
``"y ~ w + (endog = z)"`` -- see the module docstring.

Agreement
---------
On the fixture data (100 firms x 7 years) StataNow 19.5 reports ``fe``:
endog 1.102058 (se .0694014), w .5391216 (se .0502034), _cons 1.014978
(se .0387732); ``re``: endog 1.120466 (se .065102), w .5286517
(se .0482393), _cons 1.014533 (se .0486261).  westata reproduces all twelve
coefficients and standard errors to the printed precision.
exports.signature: (endog: 'Any', exog: 'Any', endog_regressors: 'Any', instruments: 'Any', *, exog_names: 'Sequence[str]', endog_names: 'Sequence[str]', instrument_names: 'Sequence[str]', codes: 'np.ndarray', sizes: 'np.ndarray', method: 'str' = 'fe', model_data: 'pd.DataFrame | None' = None) -> 'None'
exports.from_formula: (formula: 'str', data: 'pd.DataFrame', *, entity: 'str', time: 'str | None' = None, method: 'str' = 'fe', subset: 'Any' = None) -> "'XtIvreg'"
exports.fit: (self, cov_type: 'str' = 'nonrobust', cov_kwds: 'Mapping[str, Any] | None' = None, ssc: 'Any' = None, *, maxiter: 'int' = 100, strict: 'bool' = False) -> 'StataResults'

exports.name: XtLogit
exports.docstring:
Panel logit (Stata ``xtlogit``), ``fe`` / ``re`` / ``pa``.

``model_name`` is ``"xtlogit, fe"``, ``"xtlogit, re"`` or ``"xtlogit, pa"``
depending on ``method``; all three report ``dist="z"`.

``method="fe"``
    Chamberlain's conditional likelihood.  Groups with a constant outcome are
    dropped, ``e(N_drop)``/``e(N_group_drop)`` record how many observations
    and groups that costs, there is no intercept, and ``e(chi2type)`` is
    ``"LR"``.  ``e(ll_0)`` is the intercept-only logit on the *retained*
    observations, which is what makes ``e(chi2)`` reproduce Stata's
    ``LR chi2(2) = 32.46``.
``method="re"``
    Integrated likelihood with a Gaussian random effect, adaptive
    Gauss-Hermite.  ``/lnsig2u`` is a parameter in ``e(b)`` (as Stata stores
    it, and as this module labels it); ``e(sigma_u)`` and ``e(rho)`` hold
    the derived quantities.
``method="pa"``
    GEE with an exchangeable working correlation.  **Not a likelihood**: no
    ``e(ll)``, ``e(ll_0)``, ``e(r2_p)``, ``e(aic)``/``e(bic)``, and the model
    test is ``e(chi2type)="Wald"``.  ``e(estimator)="gee"`` marks it.

exports.name: XtNbreg
exports.docstring:
Conditional fixed-effects negative binomial (Stata ``xtnbreg, fe``).

Stata maximises the Hausman-Hall-Griliches (1984) conditional kernel

    ``q_i(b) = sum_t ln Gamma(lam_it + y_it) - ln Gamma(lam_it) - ln Gamma(y_it+1)
               + ln Gamma(sum_t lam_it) + ln Gamma(S_i + 1)
               - ln Gamma(sum_t lam_it + S_i)``

with ``lam_it = exp(x_it'b)`` and ``S_i = sum_t y_it`` (``xtnb_fe.ado`` in
Stata's own source).  This is *not* the conditional Poisson kernel: the
negative-binomial dispersion enters through the ``ln Gamma(lam + y) -
ln Gamma(lam)`` terms, which is why ``xtnbreg, fe`` and ``xtpoisson, fe``
report different standard errors (``.07070`` vs ``.06590``).

``_cons`` is part of the parameter vector, exactly as in Stata, which prints
``_cons = 15.21552`` with a standard error of ``641``.  The likelihood is
nearly flat in that direction (adding a constant to every ``lam_it`` leaves
``q_i`` unchanged in the large-``lam`` limit), so its estimate is
optimiser-dependent while the slopes are not.  Dropping the constant instead
- the previous version of this module did - is *not* a harmless
reparameterisation: it moves the slope from ``.50418`` to ``.51711``, i.e.
2.6e-2 away from Stata.

Agreement, and why the tolerance matters
----------------------------------------
**This estimator's residual against Stata is Stata's convergence criterion,
not a likelihood difference.  Do not "fix" it again.**

The evidence is that the observed information is exact.  Evaluating this
module's analytic Hessian at **Stata's own ``e(b)``** reproduces Stata's
``e(V)`` to ``3.67e-13 / 2.97e-12 / 7.02e-9`` on the three parameters of a
30 x 6 panel - i.e. given the same point, both sides agree bit for bit.
Everything else is *where the optimiser stops*, and Stata's own two
tolerance settings do not agree with each other:

.. code-block:: none

    xtnbreg yc x1 x2, fe                      b = [.35844983, -.22522002, 7.10468266]
    xtnbreg yc x1 x2, fe ltolerance(1e-8)     b = [.35845171, -.22524727, 7.18542849]

The intercepts differ by 1.1e-2 and the slopes by 4.7e-6 / 1.05e-4 - *between
two Stata runs of the same command*, because the HHG kernel is essentially
flat in the intercept (that is why Stata prints ``e(_cons)`` SE = 641,
``z`` = 0.02).  Chasing Stata's default printout is therefore chasing a
stopping rule.

Measured agreement, 100 x 7 fixture panel (``p9_outputs.txt`` line 325) and
the 30 x 6 panel:

================================  ==========  ==============================
quantity                          fixture     note
================================  ==========  ==============================
slope vs ``ltolerance(1e-8)``     7.0e-9      the comparison that is meaningful
slope vs Stata's default printout 2.1e-5      Stata stops at ``1e-7`` first
SE vs ``ltolerance(1e-8)``        1.9e-6      observed information slope block
SE evaluated at Stata's own b     3.7e-13     the information matrix itself
``e(ll)`` vs ``ltolerance(1e-8)`` 3.5e-9      ``-775.440679``
================================  ==========  ==============================

Hence the acceptance criterion recorded in ``retest/fix/panel/FIXES.md`` is
**B tier: slopes within 1e-6 of ``xtnbreg, fe ltolerance(1e-8)``**, not of
the default printout.  Reported as
``e(estimator) = "hhg_conditional_ml"``; ``e(quasi_likelihood) = 1`` keeps
the value from being read as a full likelihood of the data.

The solver stops on the gradient (Stata's ``nrtolerance`` rule) with
``lstsq`` rather than ``solve``, because the information matrix really is
near-singular in the intercept direction; the kernel is accumulated as
``sum_{j<y} log(lam + j)`` rather than as differences of ``lgamma``, which
would lose every digit once ``lam`` enters the ``1e7`` range.
exports.signature: (endog: 'Any', exog: 'Any', groups: 'Any', *, param_names: 'Sequence[str]', method: 'str', model_data: 'pd.DataFrame | None' = None) -> 'None'
exports.from_formula: (formula: 'str', data: 'pd.DataFrame', *, entity: 'str', time: 'str | None' = None, method: 'str' = 'fe', subset: 'Any' = None) -> "'XtNbreg'"

exports.name: XtPcse
exports.docstring:
Panel-corrected standard errors (Stata ``xtpcse``), Beck-Katz (1995).

OLS point estimates with the panel-corrected VCE.  ``[XT] xtpcse`` Methods and
formulas gives

.. math:: V(\hat\beta) = (X'X)^{-1} X'\Omega X (X'X)^{-1},
          \qquad \hat\Sigma_{ij} = e_i'e_j / T_{ij}.

**No small-sample factor is applied.**  The P9 plan specifies
``N/(N-k) * T/(T-1)``; that is not in the manual, and on the fixture data the
uncorrected formula reproduces Stata's ``e(V)`` to 3e-12 while the plan's
factor (1.16999) would inflate both standard errors by 8.2%.  The empirical
check lives in ``tests/test_panel_iv.py``.

``Omega`` is assembled exactly as Stata's ``xtpcse.ado`` assembles it, which
matters on unbalanced panels and is *not* the naive ``Sigma kron I``:

* ``casewise`` (Stata's default) estimates ``Sigma`` from the periods common
  to **every** panel - ``e(n_sigma)`` periods, and Stata warns when that is
  under half of ``e(n_avg)`` - but accumulates ``X'Omega X`` over **all**
  observations.  ``e(Sigma)`` from Stata matches the casewise estimator to
  2.7e-15 and ``e(V)`` to 4.3e-18 on a 20-panel 4-8 period panel.
* ``pairwise`` uses, for each ``(i, j)``, the periods those two panels share:
  ``T_ij`` in the denominator.  Stata's ``e(Sigma)`` matches to 1.8e-15 and
  ``e(V)`` to 8.7e-18 on the same data.

The accumulation itself follows Stata's ``matrix glsaccum ..., row(ivar)
group(timevar)``: it is grouped by *period*, and within a period the
``Sigma`` sub-block is selected by the panels observed then.  Summing
``sigma_ij * X_i'X_j`` over panel pairs instead hard-codes the balanced case
and is wrong as soon as a period is missing from one panel.

When ``time=`` may be omitted
-----------------------------
``from_formula(..., time=...)`` is optional here, unlike Stata which requires
``tis`` for ``xtpcse``.  The rule is:

* **Balanced panel (every entity has the same number of rows): ``time=`` may
  be omitted.**  Periods are then read *positionally* - the first
  observation of each entity is period 0, the second period 1, and so on.
  For a panel built entity-by-entity in row order that is exactly the period
  grid Stata sees, and omitting ``time=`` gives bit-identical results to
  passing it (verified on a 100 x 7 panel: ``x1 = .75331259`` with
  ``se = .05643178``, ``_cons = 1.57268563`` with ``se = .03729976``,
  ``e(n_sigma) = 7``, both ways).

  This matters because the positional grid is only *implicit*: it assumes
  the rows really are ordered ``entity-major, period-minor``, which is what
  :func:`_as_frame` guarantees.

* **Unbalanced panel and no ``time=``: rejected** with
  :class:`~westata.errors.ConsistencyError` naming ``time=``.  Pairing by
  position would compare one entity's third observation against another's
  fifth, which is not a covariance at all - silently returning that number
  under an ``xtpcse`` label is the failure mode this module exists to avoid.

* **Unbalanced panel with ``time=`` given but no period common to all
  panels: rejected** with the ``casewise`` message, mirroring Stata's
  ``r(459)`` ("no time periods are common to all panels, cannot estimate
  disturbance covariance matrix using casewise inclusion") and, like Stata,
  pointing at ``selection="pairwise"`` - which does not need common periods
  and succeeds on such data.

``correlation(ar1/psar1)`` - which replaces OLS with Prais-Winsten - raises
:class:`westata.errors.UnsupportedError`.
exports.signature: (endog: 'Any', exog: 'Any', codes: 'np.ndarray', sizes: 'np.ndarray', *, param_names: 'Sequence[str]', correlation: 'str' = 'independent', selection: 'str' = 'casewise', periods: 'np.ndarray | None' = None, model_data: 'pd.DataFrame | None' = None) -> 'None'

exports.name: XtPoisson
exports.docstring:
Panel Poisson (Stata ``xtpoisson``), ``fe`` / ``re``.

``method="fe"``
    Conditioning on the group total ``S_i = sum_t y_it`` removes ``alpha_i``
    exactly (the multinomial reduction), so this is a genuine likelihood:

        ``ln L = sum_i [ sum_t y_it x_it'b - S_i ln sum_t exp(x_it'b)
                  + ln S_i! - sum_t ln y_it! ]``

    Groups with ``S_i = 0`` carry no information and are dropped.  Verified
    against ``p9_outputs.txt`` lines 226-250: ``.5041803`` (se
    ``.0344352``), log likelihood ``-775.44068`` - every printed digit.
``method="re"``
    The gamma random effect is conjugate to the Poisson, so the group
    likelihood is available in closed form and no quadrature is involved:

        ``l_i = sum_t [y_it ln mu_it - ln y_it!]
                + ln Gamma(S_i + 1/a) - ln Gamma(1/a) - (1/a) ln a
                - (S_i + 1/a) ln(M_i + 1/a)``

    with ``M_i = sum_t mu_it`` and ``a`` the gamma dispersion
    (``Var = a``, Stata's ``alpha``).  Reported as ``/lnalpha``, which is
    how Stata stores it.  Verified: ``.4795509`` / ``.3485993`` /
    ``-2.073955``, log likelihood ``-1076.9058``.

exports.name: XtTobit
exports.docstring:
Random-effects Tobit (Stata ``xttobit``).

``y*_it = x_it'b + u_i + e_it`` with ``u_i ~ N(0, sigma_u^2)`` and
``e_it ~ N(0, sigma_e^2)``; the observed outcome is censored at ``lower``
and/or ``upper``.  Both variance components are estimated and reported as
``/sigma_u`` and ``/sigma_e`` (Stata's own labels, and the scale Stata stores
them on), with ``e(rho) = sigma_u^2/(sigma_u^2 + sigma_e^2)``.

Quadrature accuracy
-------------------
``intpoints=12`` is Stata's default and this module's default, and with the
*adaptive* rule it is already sufficient here: on the P9 fixture panel
(100 firms x 7 years, ``ll(.5)``) the estimates are stable to 7 digits for
every ``intpoints`` from 8 upwards.

===========  ==========  ==========  ==========  ===========
intpoints    x1          _cons       log L       sigma_u
===========  ==========  ==========  ==========  ===========
8            .9020131    .9253713    -598.85059  .4883512
10           .9020131    .9253712    -598.85058  .4883516
12           .9020131    .9253712    -598.85058  .4883516
30           .9020131    .9253712    -598.85058  .4883516
50           .9020131    .9253712    -598.85058  .4883516
Stata        .9020131    .9253712    -598.85058  .4883516
===========  ==========  ==========  ==========  ===========

A *non-adaptive* rule is what needs 30+ points here; the adaptation is what
buys the accuracy, not the node count.  That is why
:func:`_adaptive_log_integral_batch` follows Stata's Naylor-Smith centring
literally instead of reaching for more quadrature points.

exports.name: XtUnitroot
exports.docstring:
Panel unit-root tests (Stata ``xtunitroot ips`` / ``xtunitroot llc``).

Both are panel-wide Dickey-Fuller procedures, and both match Stata on the
fixture data because the look-up tables are transcribed rather than re-derived.

``ips`` (Im-Pesaran-Shin; balanced, no lags by default)
    Per panel, ``Delta y_it`` is regressed on ``y_i,t-1`` and a panel constant,
    giving ``t_i``.  Stata reports three statistics:

    * ``t-bar = mean(t_i)`` -- exact finite-``N`` tabulated critical values, and
      no p-value;
    * ``t-tilde-bar = mean(t_i * s_i / sigma(y_i))``, where ``s_i`` is the ADF
      residual RMSE -- Stata's small-``T`` variant;
    * ``Z-t-tilde-bar = sqrt(N)(t-tilde-bar - E)/sqrt(V)`` with ``E`` and ``V``
      interpolated from IPS (2003) table 3 at ``T`` -- the one with a p-value.

    On the fixture (90 panels x 9 periods) westata reproduces ``t-bar``
    -2.0685, ``t-tilde-bar`` -1.5727 and ``Z`` -4.2953.

``llc`` (Levin-Lin-Chu; balanced, one ADF lag by default)
    Stata's default is ``lags(1)`` with a Bartlett kernel whose bandwidth is
    ``int(3.21 * T^(1/3))`` -- 6 at ``T = 9``, which is why the fixture header
    prints "6.00 lags average".  The adjusted statistic is
    ``t* = (t - N*Tbar*sbar/Var_ep * se(t) * mu) / sigma`` with ``(mu, sigma)``
    interpolated from LLC (2002) table 2.  On the fixture westata reproduces
    ``Unadjusted t = -21.7694`` and ``Adjusted t* = -15.1701``.

Both tests require a strongly balanced panel with no gaps -- Stata's
requirement too (``_xtstrbal``).  An unbalanced panel raises
:class:`westata.errors.ConsistencyError` rather than silently using whichever
rows happen to line up.  ``trend``, ``noconstant``, ``demean`` and
information-criterion lag selection raise
:class:`westata.errors.UnsupportedError`.

exports.name: Xtdidregress
exports.docstring:
Panel difference-in-differences (Stata ``xtdidregress``).

The estimator is the same two-way fixed-effects regression as
:class:`Didregress`, and the ATET is identical on a balanced panel.  Only
the degrees-of-freedom convention differs, and for the reason Stata
documents: a panel unit effect is nested in the ``group()`` cluster
variable, so it adds nothing to the ``(N-1)/(N-K)`` factor.  The clustered
standard error is therefore the smaller one Stata prints -- ``.055228``
against ``.0590465`` for ``didregress`` on the P11 fixture.

Unlike ``didregress`` this spelling requires a genuine panel: each
``(group, time)`` cell may occur at most once, matching Stata's ``xtset``
requirement ("repeated time values within panel").  Unbalanced panels are
estimated (the within transform handles them); the exact agreement with
:class:`Didregress` is guaranteed, and tested, for balanced panels.

exports.docstring:
Adjust a family of p-values with Stata's ``_mtest`` methods.

Parameters
----------
pvalues:
    Raw p-values, one per test.
method:
    ``"bonferroni"``, ``"holm"``, ``"sidak"`` or ``"noadjust"``.

Returns
-------
numpy.ndarray
    Adjusted p-values in the SAME order as the input.

Raises
------
ValueError
    For an unknown method.

Notes
-----
``noadjust`` returns the raw values, which is what ``_mtest.ado:212`` does
when no method is requested.

exports.name: check_time_spacing
exports.docstring:
Classify the spacing of ``time_values``; ``Checkt`` (``newey.ado:263-290``).

Returns
-------
(tflag, delta)
    ``tflag`` is 0 (regular, interval 1), 1 (irregular) or 2 (regular but
    interval > 1).  ``delta`` is the common interval when regular, else
    ``None``.

Notes
-----
Stata reads ``_dta[_TSdelta]`` (the delta from ``tsset``) and divides the
first differences by it.  With no delta set it uses 1.  Both the min and max
of those scaled differences are then compared:

* ``r(min) != r(max)``              -> ``tflag = 1`` (irregular)
* ``r(mean) > 1 & r(min) == r(max)`` -> ``tflag = 2`` (interval > 1)

Because a ``pd.Timedelta`` or a float delta both work, the caller's array is
converted to float first and differences are taken on the ROW ORDER, matching
Stata's ``sort touse tvar``.
exports.signature: (time_values: 'Any') -> 'tuple[int, float | None]'

exports.docstring:
ANOVA-style contrasts of a factor variable's estimated means.

    The factor's design-matrix prefix, e.g. ``"C(g)"`` or ``"g"``.  It is
    matched on the data variable, so ``"C(g)"`` also finds the columns of a
    model fitted with ``C(g, base='a')``.

    ``"r"`` reference (each non-reference level minus the reference level),
    ``"g"`` grand mean (each level minus the unweighted average of all
    levels), or ``"a"`` adjacent (``level[i+1] - level[i]``).  Anything else
    raises :class:`UnsupportedError`.
level:
    Confidence level as a fraction (Stata's ``level(95)`` -> ``0.95``).

Returns
-------
list[LincomResult]
    One row per comparison, in level order: ``L - 1`` rows for ``"r"`` and
    ``"a"``, ``L`` rows for ``"g"``.

exports.name: dfgls
exports.docstring:
DF-GLS unit-root test, as ``dfgls varname [, maxlag(#) notrend]``.

**Stata defaults to a TREND, not to no trend.** ``dfgls.ado:39-46`` sets ``trend=1`` unless
the user writes ``notrend``; the earlier version of this function defaulted to ``False`` and
so implemented Stata's ``notrend`` case while being compared against Stata's default output.
That single inverted default is the whole reason rounds 119-123 spent five rounds seeing
tau +0.806 against Stata's -1.284 and concluding the algorithm was unexplainable.

Measured on nelson_plosser.dta's lrgnp (both from live Stata):

    dfgls lrgnp             lag 10  tau = -1.284   (default, trend)
    dfgls lrgnp, notrend    lag 10  tau = +0.806   (the no-trend case)

``trend=False`` selects the second. With the trend the detrending uses
``cbar=-13.5`` and subtracts ``b_iota + b_qdtrd*t``; without it, ``cbar=-7`` and only
``b_iota``. Both cases reproduce Stata to the printed digit.

``maxlag=None`` uses Schwert's rule ``int(12*(n/100)**0.25)`` (``dfgls.ado:64``).

``notrend=`` was REMOVED (R3.1): it and ``trend=`` set the same state, and having two
switches made ``notrend=False`` a no-op that nevertheless looked meaningful.  Stata
spells the option ``notrend``; the Python argument is the positive ``trend``, and
``notrend=True`` is still accepted for one release as a deprecation shim.
exports.signature: (series: 'Any', *, maxlag: 'int | None' = None, trend: 'bool' = True, name: 'str' = '', **legacy: 'Any') -> 'DFGLSResult'

exports.name: dfuller
exports.docstring:
Augmented Dickey-Fuller test, spelled the way Stata spells it.

A thin alias: ``dfuller(y, trend=True)`` is ``unitroot(y, test="adf", regression="ct")``.
It exists because ``unitroot`` is not the name a Stata user reaches for, and the option
mapping is not guessable:

    no option     ->  regression="c"
    , trend       ->  regression="ct"
    , noconstant  ->  regression="n"

Measured against a live Stata on nelson_plosser.dta, where the numbers already matched:

    dfuller lrgnp, trend    Z(t) -2.026     unitroot(..., regression="ct")  -2.0262
    dfuller d.lrgnp         Z(t) -5.322     unitroot(..., regression="c")   -5.3216

``lags=`` maps to ``maxlag``; Stata's default is zero lags, which is what ``None`` gives.
Passing ``regression=`` overrides ``trend``.
exports.signature: (endog: 'Any', *, trend: 'bool' = False, lags: 'int | None' = None, autolag: 'str | None' = None, regression: 'str | None' = None) -> 'UnitRootResult'

exports.name: endog_regf_test
exports.docstring:
Run ``regF``: the augmented-regression F test for endogeneity.

Parameters
----------
structure:
    The ``iv_structure`` dict (``exog``/``endog``/``instruments`` + names).
response:
    The dependent variable on the estimation sample.
cov_type:
    The VCE to use inside the augmented fit.  ``regF`` is reported for
    ``robust``, ``cluster`` and ``HAC``; an unadjusted VCE gets Durbin-Wu
    instead, so this is only called for the others.
cluster_labels:
    Required when ``cov_type`` is clustered.
tested:
    Endogenous regressors to test.  Stata requires the full set under a
    robust/cluster/HAC VCE (``ivregress_estat.ado:1070-1076``).

Raises
------
ValueError
    When there is no endogenous regressor, when ``tested`` is not the full
    set, or when a clustered VCE arrives without labels.
exports.signature: (structure: 'dict[str, Any]', response: 'np.ndarray', *, cov_type: 'str' = 'nonrobust', cluster_labels: 'Sequence[Any] | None' = None, tested: 'Sequence[str] | None' = None) -> 'RegFResult'

exports.name: endog_score_test
exports.docstring:
Run ``robwool`` (robust) or ``acwool`` (HAC).

Parameters
----------
structure:
    The ``iv_structure`` dict with ``exog``/``endog``/``instruments`` and
    their names.
resid:
    The IV residuals of the consistent (2SLS) fit.  The ado refits an OLS for
    ``uhat``; on the estimation sample that is the same residual series only
    when ``exog`` spans the same space, so the caller passes the consistent
    residuals explicitly.
response:
    The dependent variable, used to rebuild ``uhat`` exactly as the ado does.
hac:
    Use the HAC variant (prewhiten the ``rhat`` columns).
lags:
    HAC truncation; ignored unless ``hac`` is true.
tested:
    Endogenous regressors to test.  Stata refuses a subset under a
    robust/cluster/HAC VCE (``ivregress_estat.ado:1070-1076``), so a subset
    longer or shorter than the full list is rejected here too.

Raises
------
ValueError

    when no endogenous regressor is present.

exports.name: estat_auc
exports.docstring:
Area under the ROC curve for a binary-outcome fit.

Parameters
----------
result:
    A fitted ``logit``/``probit`` result.

Returns
-------
AucResult
    ``str(...)`` prints Stata's one-line note; ``.to_dict()`` gives ``r(area)`` /
    ``r(N)``.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any') -> 'AucResult'

exports.name: estat_bgodfrey
exports.docstring:
Breusch-Godfrey LM test, as ``estat bgodfrey, lags(...)``.

``result`` must be an OLS-style fit carrying residuals and the estimation design; Stata
refuses the test after ``regress, robust`` and so does this -- including
``vce(cluster)``, which Stata treats as robust.

``nomiss0`` keeps the leading missing values of the lagged residuals MISSING instead of
replacing them with zero, which shortens the auxiliary regression by ``p`` rows.
``bgodfrey.ado:180-184`` is the whole difference::

    if "`dm'"=="" {
        foreach i of local reslist {
            qui replace `i' = 0 if `i' >= . & `touse'
        }
    }

The option is called ``dm`` inside the ado -- "Davidson-MacKinnon method is now
miss0" -- so an empty macro means the default (replace with zero) and a set one means
keep them missing. Measured on a 200-row series, default against ``nomiss0``:

    lag 1: chi2 187.976  ->  191.674
    lag 2: chi2 188.371  ->  191.009

Parameters
----------
time:
    Stands in for ``tsset``. Either the NAME of a column in the fit's estimation frame
    or the period values themselves, one per estimation row. When given, the lags are
    taken on the time axis: a period that is absent from the sample produces a MISSING
    lag instead of silently pairing the rows on either side. Omitting it lags by row
    order, which is only correct when the rows are already a contiguous period
    sequence. Measured on icecream.dta with ``time == 5`` dropped, Stata's
    4.220 / 4.476 / 4.787 / 5.048 against 3.286 / 3.363 / 3.403 / 5.084 by row order.
delta:
    The lag step, ``tsset``'s ``Delta:``. One unless the data declare otherwise; an
    explicit ``tsset t, delta(2)`` is the only case that differs. Must be a positive
    integer, which is ``tsset``'s own rule (r(451) for fractional periods).

Raises
------
ConsistencyError
    After a robust or clustered VCE, on a panel spanning several units, or when
    ``time`` cannot be resolved against the estimation sample.
ValueError
    For a bad lag order or a non-integer ``delta``.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', *, lags: 'int | Sequence[int]' = 1, nomiss0: 'bool' = False, time: 'str | Sequence[Any] | None' = None, delta: 'float' = 1.0) -> 'BgTestResult'

exports.name: estat_classification
exports.docstring:
Stata's ``estat classification`` after ``logit``/``probit``.

Parameters
----------
result:
    A fitted binary-outcome result.
cutoff:
    The probability threshold (Stata's ``cutoff()``); must lie in [0, 1].
y:
    The observed binary response.  When omitted it is rebuilt from the
    fitted values and residuals.
probabilities:
    The predicted probability of the positive class.  When omitted,
    ``result.predict(kind="pr")`` is used.

Raises
------
NotImplementedError
    For a model Stata does not route ``estat classification`` from.
ValueError
    For a cutoff outside [0, 1], or when the response is not binary.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', *, cutoff: 'float' = 0.5, y: 'Any' = None, probabilities: 'Any' = None) -> 'ClassificationResult'

exports.name: estat_corrgram
exports.docstring:
``corrgram``: autocorrelations, partial autocorrelations and Q at each lag.

``corrgram.ado:68`` accumulates ``Q = n(n+2) sum ac^2/(n-k)`` as it goes, so the Q column
is the Ljung-Box statistic using lags ``1..k`` -- which is why the last row equals what
``wntestq`` reports for the same order.

The default order is ``max(1, min(int(n/2) - 2, 40))`` (``corrgram.ado:18``), not a
function of the previous regression's parameter count.

``time`` stands in for ``tsset``; see :func:`estat_dwatson`.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', *, lags: 'int | None' = None, time: 'str | Any | None' = None, delta: 'float' = 1.0) -> 'Correlogram'

exports.name: estat_dwatson
exports.docstring:
Durbin-Watson d.

.. math:: d = \sum_{t=2}^{n}(e_t - e_{t-1})^2 / \sum_{t=1}^{n} e_t^2

Measured on icecream.dta after ``reg consumption temp price income``: 1.021169.

``time`` stands in for ``tsset`` and is what decides which differences exist: with a
period missing from the sample, the pair straddling the gap is dropped rather than
differenced, because ``L.`` is undefined across it. Measured on icecream.dta with
``time == 5`` dropped: Stata reports ``.8930395``, and differencing adjacent ROWS gives
``1.0868969``.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', *, time: 'str | Any | None' = None, delta: 'float' = 1.0) -> 'DurbinWatsonResult'

exports.name: estat_endogenous
exports.docstring:
Stata's ``estat endogenous``.

Which test comes back depends on the VCE
(``ivregress_estat.ado:1128-1145``):

==============  =========================================================
``vce``         reported
==============  =========================================================
unadjusted      Durbin-Wu (``durbin``, ``wu``)
robust          the robust score (``robwool``)
HAC             the HAC score (``acwool``)
cluster         refused -- Stata reports only ``regF``, which needs the
                augmented regression and is not implemented here
==============  =========================================================

Parameters
----------
lags:
    HAC truncation for ``acwool``.  ``ivregress_estat.ado:1055-1063`` defaults
    it to 1 under a HAC VCE and rejects a non-positive value; ``lags`` is only
    valid with HAC.

Raises
------
NotImplementedError
    For a non-IV result.
ValueError
    When the model has no endogenous regressor, when ``lags`` is given
    without a HAC VCE, or after a clustered VCE.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', *, lags: 'int | None' = None) -> 'Any'

exports.name: estat_esize
exports.docstring:
Stata's ``estat esize``.

Parameters
----------
epsilon:
    Report epsilon-squared (``sthlp:620-622``).
omega:
    Report omega-squared (``sthlp:624-626``).  Mutually exclusive with ``epsilon``
    (``esize.ado:14``: ``opts_exclusive "`epsilon' `omega'"``).
level:
    Confidence level as a FRACTION (``0.95``), never a percentage (R3.3).

    This used to default to ``95.0``.  Every other ``level`` in the package is a
    fraction (``margins``, ``nlcom``, ``lincom_as_stata``, ``contrast``), so a
    caller who passed ``level=0.95`` here got ``(100 - 0.95) / 2 = 49.5%``
    intervals -- a plausible-looking number, silently wrong.  Verified: the old
    expression printed ``[49.5% Conf. Interval]``.

Raises
------
NotImplementedError
    When the fit is not ``regress`` or ``anova`` -- ``sthlp:599-601`` restricts it.
ValueError
    When both ``epsilon`` and ``omega`` are requested.

Notes
-----
``regress`` stores ``e(mss)`` and ``e(rss)`` but NOT ``e(tss)``, so the total is
reconstructed as their sum.  That is an identity for a model with a constant; a
``noconstant`` fit has no such decomposition, which is why Stata's own total is not
consulted here.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', *, epsilon: 'bool' = False, omega: 'bool' = False, level: 'float' = 0.95) -> 'EffectSizeResult'

exports.name: estat_firststage
exports.docstring:
Stata's ``estat firststage`` for an IV fit.

Parameters
----------
all:
    Stata's ``all`` option: report the R-squared block even when the model has MORE
    than one endogenous regressor.  ``ivregress_postestimation.sthlp:408-414`` says
    the default switches to Shea's partial R-squared in that case, and that ``all``
    asks for every first-stage statistic "regardless of whether the model contains
    one or more endogenous regressors".
forcenonrobust:
    Stata's ``forcenonrobust`` option (``sthlp:416-422``): report the minimum
    eigenvalue statistic and its critical values even though a robust VCE was used.
    Without it those numbers are suppressed under a robust VCE, because the critical
    values assume independent, identically distributed normal errors.

Raises
------
NotImplementedError
    When the result carries no IV structure.
ValueError
    When the model has no endogenous regressor, or no excluded instrument
    (in which case the first stage is not identified).
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', *, all: 'bool' = False, forcenonrobust: 'bool' = False) -> 'FirstStageResult'

exports.name: estat_gof
exports.docstring:
Stata's ``estat gof`` after ``poisson``.

Parameters
----------
result:
    A fitted :class:`~westata.estimators.discrete.Poisson` result.
y, mu:
    The response and the fitted mean.  ``mu`` defaults to
    ``result.fittedvalues``; ``y`` defaults to ``mu + result.resid`` (which
    is exact for these fits).  Pass them explicitly when the result does not
    retain a usable residual.

Returns

GofResult

Raises

NotImplementedError

exports.name: estat_hettest
exports.docstring:
Stata's ``estat hettest`` (Breusch-Pagan / Cook-Weisberg).

Parameters
----------
result:
    A fitted linear result that retained its design, residuals and weights.
method:
    ``"normal"`` (default) reports ``e(mss)/2``; ``"iid"`` reports
    ``e(N)*e(r2)``; ``"fstat"`` reports the auxiliary regression's ``F``.
variables:
    Design columns for the auxiliary regression, named exactly as they appear
    in ``result.design_matrix[1]`` (a factor level is e.g.
    ``"foreign[T.Foreign]"``).  ``None`` or an empty sequence regresses on
    the **fitted values**, which is Stata's behaviour with no varlist -- it
    is not "all regressors"; use ``rhs=True`` for that.
rhs:
    Stata's ``, rhs``: add every non-constant regressor to the auxiliary
    regression (``hettest.ado:69-76``).  Combines with ``variables`` as a
    union, exactly as the ado does.
mtest:
    Request the per-regressor multiple-testing table.  As in
    ``hettest.ado:126-128``, a single-regressor auxiliary regression drops
    ``mtest()`` silently and only the simultaneous test is returned.

Raises
------
ValueError
    For a robust/clustered VCE, pweighted data, a noconstant fit, an
    inconsistent ``method``/option combination, or when the design was not
    retained.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', *, method: 'str' = 'normal', variables: 'Sequence[str] | None' = None, rhs: 'bool' = False, mtest: 'str | None' = None) -> 'Any'

exports.name: estat_ic
exports.docstring:
Stata's ``estat ic`` for one fitted model.

Parameters
----------
result:
    A fitted result carrying ``e(ll)`` (and optionally ``e(ll_0)``).
n:
    Override ``N`` used by BIC/AICc/CAIC (Stata's ``n(#)``).
df:
    Override the degrees-of-freedom count used by all four criteria
    (Stata's ``df(#)``).

Raises
------
ValueError
    When the model has no log-likelihood (a criterion cannot be built for a
    fit that is not maximum likelihood), or ``N``/``df`` cannot be resolved.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', *, n: 'float | None' = None, df: 'float | None' = None) -> 'IcResult'

exports.name: estat_imtest
exports.docstring:
Stata's ``estat imtest`` after ``regress``.

Parameters
----------
result:
    A fitted linear result carrying the residuals and ``e(rss)``/``e(N)``.
white:
    Also compute White's original test (Stata's ``, white``).
design:
    Optional design matrix including the constant.  Defaults to
    ``result.design_matrix``.

Raises
------
NotImplementedError
    For a model other than ``regress``.
ValueError
    For weighted data, a clustered VCE, a model with no covariates, or when
    the design was not retained.

Notes
-----
Weights and ``cluster()`` are refused because ``imtest.ado:18-25`` refuses
them; there the statistic would be computed from the unweighted residual
geometry and mean something else.

**Precision.** ``imtest.ado:35`` computes in FLOAT unless ``, double`` is
given, so Stata's DEFAULT ``r(chi2)`` differs from an exact computation in
roughly the 8th significant digit -- measured on ``regress mpg weight
foreign``: default ``9.794147910432786`` against ``, double``
``9.794148277797737``.  This module always computes in double precision,
which means it agrees with ``estat imtest, white double`` to machine
precision and with the default only to ~1e-8.  That is deliberate: float32
accumulation is a property of Stata's storage type, not of the statistic,
and emulating it bit-for-bit would make the answer depend on rounding order.
The committed fixture records BOTH columns
(``tests/conformance/stata_fixtures/imtest_auto.json``) so the difference is
documented rather than argued about.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', *, white: 'bool' = False, design: 'Any' = None) -> 'ImTestResult'

exports.name: estat_moran
exports.docstring:
Stata's ``estat moran``.

Parameters
----------
errorlag:
    One spatial weighting matrix, or a sequence of them for a higher-order test
    (``sthlp:66-68``: "``errorlag()`` is required ... repeatable to allow testing of
    higher-order error lags").  Repeated matrices are SUMMED, which is how Stata
    combines several ``spmatrix`` objects into one lag operator.
weights:
    Alias for ``errorlag`` -- ``errorlag`` is Stata's option name, ``weights`` reads
    better in Python.  Supplying both is an error.

Raises
------
NotImplementedError
    When the fit is not a linear regression (``sthlp:44-45``).
ValueError
    When no weighting matrix is given, when it does not match the estimation sample,
    or when the statistic is undefined.

Notes
-----
See the module docstring: Stata's own ``r(chi2)`` formula is not locally available
(the methods section is external and the ado is a compiled builtin), so the reported
statistic is the standard randomisation-based Moran test.  Its p-value is exact for
the hypothesis "no spatial correlation", but it may differ from Stata's number.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', errorlag: 'Any' = None, *, weights: 'Any' = None) -> 'MoranResult'

exports.name: estat_mundlak
exports.docstring:
Stata's ``estat mundlak``.

Parameters
----------
result:
    A fit from :class:`westata.RandomEffects` (or any panel estimator that recorded
    ``panel_entity``).
storer:
    Callback used to fit the augmented equation.  It receives the augmented frame
    and returns a fitted result.  Highest priority when given.
entity, time:
    The panel identifier and time name for the AUGMENTED refit.  Required when
    ``storer`` is omitted: the fitted result keeps ``panel_entity`` (the coded group
    labels) but not the column names the estimator's ``from_formula`` needs, so the
    test cannot rebuild the equation without them.

Raises
------
NotImplementedError
    For a non-panel result.
ValueError
    When the estimation data or the panel identifier is unavailable, when the model
    has no slopes to test, or when ``entity``/``time`` are needed but missing.

Notes
-----
``sthlp:369-370`` rules out ``absorb()`` and ``vce(hc2)``: the first has no
group-mean interpretation and the second has no likelihood to re-estimate.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', *, storer: 'Any' = None, entity: 'str | None' = None, time: 'str | None' = None) -> 'MundlakResult'

exports.name: estat_overid
exports.docstring:
Stata's ``estat overid``.

Parameters
----------
lags:
    HAC truncation for the prewhitening step.  Stata's ``OverID2sls``
    (``ivregress_estat.ado:84-95``) defaults this to **1** for a HAC VCE and
    rejects a negative value; ``lags()`` is only meaningful with HAC, which
    the ado enforces with "lags() only valid with models with HAC VCEs".
    ``None`` selects Stata's default: 1 under HAC, 0 otherwise.
forcenonrobust:
    Stata's ``forcenonrobust`` option
    (``ivregress_postestimation.sthlp:443-451``): perform the Sargan and Basmann
    tests after 2SLS or LIML even though a robust VCE was used.  Both assume
    independent, identically distributed normal errors, which is why a robust VCE
    replaces them with Wooldridge's score test by default.

Raises
------
NotImplementedError
    For a non-IV result.
ValueError
    When the model is exactly identified, when the VCE is clustered
    (``ivregress_estat.ado:290-296`` offers no test there), when ``lags`` is
    negative, or when ``lags`` is given for a non-HAC VCE.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', *, lags: 'int | None' = None, forcenonrobust: 'bool' = False) -> 'OverIdResult'

exports.name: estat_ovtest
exports.docstring:
Stata's ``estat ovtest`` (Ramsey RESET).

Parameters
----------
result:
    A fitted linear result that retained its design and residuals.
rhs:
    Stata's ``, rhs``: test powers of the right-hand-side variables instead
    of powers of the fitted values.

Raises
------
ValueError
    When the design was not retained, when every regressor is an indicator
    (so no powers exist), or when the auxiliary fit has no residual df.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', *, rhs: 'bool' = False) -> 'OvTestResult'

exports.name: estat_ptrends
exports.docstring:
`estat ptrends` after `didregress`: the parallel-trends test over the pretreatment periods.

Stata, on a 60-group / 15-period panel with 20 treated (synthetic, seeded):

    Parallel-trends test (pretreatment time period)
    H0: Linear trends are parallel

    F(1, 59) =   0.25
    Prob > F = 0.6182

`F(1, 59)` reads as ONE linear-trend interaction against `n_groups - 1` denominator degrees of
freedom. Restricting to the periods before anyone is treated and testing whether the treated
group's linear time trend differs from the controls' is exactly that: a single interaction,
`treated_indicator * period`, with the group and period effects absorbed by the panel.

THE FIRST PROTOTYPE FOR THIS FAILED and the reason is worth keeping: putting BOTH the treatment
dummy and the interaction into the pretreatment subsample makes them collinear -- before
treatment begins the dummy is constant within group and the interaction is the dummy times the
period -- so the design is rank deficient. Only the interaction belongs in the design.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any') -> 'dict[str, float]'

exports.name: estat_summarize
exports.docstring:
Stata's ``estat summarize``.

Parameters
----------
data:
    The estimation-sample frame.  Defaults to ``result.model_data``; it must
    be supplied when the estimator did not retain one.
variables:
    Variables to summarize.  Defaults to the response plus the reported
    regressors.
weights, weight_type:
    Optional weights, with the Stata type.  ``fweight`` inflates ``Obs``;
    ``aweight``/``pweight``/``iweight`` do not (``estat_summ.ado:222-233``).
cluster, cluster_name:
    Optional cluster labels; adds the ``Obs per cluster`` block.

Raises
------
ValueError
    When the estimation data cannot be resolved, or a named variable is
    absent.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', *, data: 'pd.DataFrame | None' = None, variables: 'Sequence[str] | None' = None, weights: 'Any' = None, weight_type: 'str | None' = None, cluster: 'Any' = None, cluster_name: 'str' = '', noweights: 'bool' = False, noheader: 'bool' = False, labels: 'Mapping[str, str] | None' = None) -> 'SummarizeResult'

exports.name: estat_szroeter
exports.docstring:
Stata's ``estat szroeter``.

Parameters
----------
variables:
    Variables to test.  Either this or ``rhs`` must be given
    (``sthlp:509-510``).
rhs:
    Test the regression's own explanatory variables (``sthlp:528-530``).
mtest:
    Multiple-testing adjustment: ``bonferroni``, ``holm``, ``sidak`` or
    ``noadjust`` (``sthlp:533-540``).  Stata always performs multiple testing but
    adjusts nothing by default.

Raises
------
NotImplementedError
    When the fit is not a linear regression, is weighted, or clustered --
    ``szroeter.ado:13-21`` refuses all three.
ValueError
