Notes
-----
``szroeter.ado:13-21``: "szroeter is only possible after regress", "does not allow
weights", "does not allow cluster()".  Refusing here matches Stata rather than
silently computing a statistic whose reference distribution does not apply.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', variables: 'Sequence[str] | None' = None, *, rhs: 'bool' = False, mtest: 'str | None' = None) -> 'SzroeterResult | SzroeterTable'

exports.name: estat_vce
exports.docstring:
Stata's ``estat vce`` / ``estat vce, correlation``.

Parameters
----------
result:
    Any fitted westata result exposing ``param_names`` and
    ``cov_params()``.
correlation:
    When true, print the coefficient correlation matrix instead of the
    covariance matrix.  The diagonal is blanked to ``0`` exactly as Stata
    does.

Returns
-------
VceMatrix
    Call ``str(...)`` for the printed table, or ``.to_frame()`` for the full
    symmetric matrix.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', *, correlation: 'bool' = False) -> 'VceMatrix'

exports.name: estat_vif
exports.docstring:
Stata's ``estat vif`` for a linear fit.

Parameters
----------
result:
    A fitted linear result that retained its design (``design_matrix``).
uncentered:
    Do not centre the auxiliary regressions (Stata's ``, uncentered``).
    Required if the model has no constant, mirroring ``vif.ado``'s refusal.
nosort:
    Keep the model's own regressor order instead of sorting by VIF
    (Stata's ``, nosort``).

Returns
-------
VifResult

Raises
------
NotImplementedError
    For a non-linear model, where Stata has no ``estat vif``.
ValueError
    If the design was not retained, or if a model without a constant is
    queried without ``uncentered=True``.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', *, uncentered: 'bool' = False, nosort: 'bool' = False) -> 'VifResult'

exports.name: estat_weakrobust
exports.docstring:
Stata's ``estat weakrobust``.

Parameters
----------
ar:
    Force the Anderson-Rubin test.  It is also the default for a just-identified
    model (``sthlp:365-367``).
clr:
    Request the conditional likelihood-ratio test.  Accepted so the option is
    recognised, then refused with the reason -- see the module docstring.
betanull:
    The null hypothesis on the endogenous coefficients
    (``sthlp:457-485``).  Three accepted forms, matching Stata:

    * a mapping ``{name: value}`` -- coefficients named explicitly, others zero;
    * a sequence of numbers -- assigned BY POSITION, which is what Stata's
      ``copy`` suboption means;
    * ``None`` -- every coefficient is zero, the default.

    A sequence longer or shorter than the number of endogenous regressors is
    refused, because silently padding or truncating would test a different
    hypothesis than the caller wrote.

Notes
-----
``level`` was REMOVED rather than converted.  It only ever fed Stata's ``ci``
option, which is not implemented here (it needs the inverted test, not the
statistic), so every accepted value was discarded -- a percentage default of
``95.0`` that no caller could observe.  Deleting a dead parameter is honest;
retuning its unit would have advertised a feature that does not exist (R3.3, R1.5).

``sthlp:365-373`` makes the DEFAULT depend on identification: Anderson-Rubin when
just identified, CLR when overidentified.  Since only AR is implemented, an
overidentified model without ``ar`` refuses rather than silently reporting a
different test than Stata would.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', *, ar: 'bool | None' = None, clr: 'bool | None' = None, betanull: 'Any' = None) -> 'WeakRobustResult'

exports.name: etable_as_stata
exports.docstring:
``etable`` rendered as ``esttab`` prints it.

``etable`` returns a DataFrame because that is more useful to a program; this returns the
TEXT Stata prints, which is what a comparison needs. Both are kept: neither is a
substitute for the other.
exports.signature: (results: 'Sequence[Any]', *, model_names: 'Sequence[str] | None' = None, digits: 'int' = 3, se: 'bool' = True, stars: 'bool' = True, stats: 'Sequence[tuple[str, str]] | None' = None) -> 'str'

exports.name: format_ereturn_list
exports.docstring:
Render ``ereturn list`` for a fitted result object.

``result`` must expose ``e`` (a mapping). Matrices are discovered through
``cov_params()`` (reported as ``e(V)``) and the parameter vector (``e(b)``); a result that
supplies neither simply gets no matrices block entries.

DELEGATES TO THE RESULT'S OWN RENDERER when it has one. Round 255 found this free function
and ``StataResults.ereturn_list`` had drifted apart: 38 lines against 34, no leading blank
line, a different scalar order, an extra e(sigma) row, and an e(F) that predated the
mean-square fix. A live ``ereturn list`` STARTS with a newline and prints 35 lines, which is
what the method produces -- so the method is authoritative and this wrapper follows it. The
older body is kept below only for results that are not StataResults (a duck-typed object with
just ``e`` and ``params``).
exports.signature: (result: 'Any') -> 'str'

exports.name: hausman
exports.docstring:
Hausman test of the efficient estimator's consistency (``[R] hausman``).

Parameters
----------
consistent:
    Consistent under both hypotheses but inefficient, e.g. ``xtreg, fe``.
efficient:
    Efficient under the null but inconsistent under the alternative, e.g.
    ``xtreg, re``.
sigmamore: bool, default False
    Stata's ``hausman ..., sigmamore``: rescale the CONSISTENT estimator's
    covariance by ``(s2_efficient / s2_consistent) ** 2`` before differencing,
    where ``s2`` is ``e(sigma)`` and falls back to ``e(rmse)`` when that is
    missing. Use it when the two estimators are fit on the same sample but
    the robust VCEs are not directly comparable.
sigmaless: bool, default False
    The mirror: rescale the EFFICIENT estimator's covariance by
    ``(s2_consistent / s2_efficient) ** 2``.
constant:
    Include the intercept in the comparison (Stata's ``hausman ...,
    constant``).  The default ``False`` is Stata's default and excludes it,
    because a within-transformed intercept and a GLS intercept estimate
    different population quantities.  Verified on StataNow 19.5 with a
    40-entity x 8-period panel: default ``chi2(2) = .9525460961317572``;
    ``constant`` reports ``chi2(3) = .952546096131752`` over the same
    quadratic form extended by the constant.

Raises
------
ConsistencyError
    The models were fit on different samples, or share no comparable
    coefficient (with ``constant=True`` the constant alone is not enough:
    a Hausman test of the intercept across parameterisations is undefined).

Warns
-----
RuntimeWarning
    ``V_consistent - V_efficient`` is not positive definite.  Stata then
    inverts with a generalised inverse and still reports, so this does the
    same with ``numpy.linalg.pinv``.

Notes
-----
**Clamping the statistic at 0 is deliberate, and it is an admitted
difference from Stata.**  When ``V_c - V_e`` has a negative eigenvalue the
quadratic form can come out negative.  Stata prints that negative number
(measured on the 40-entity x 8-period panel with the effect correlated with
``x1``: ``chi2(2) = -2.35424271822838``, ``r(p) = 1``) and warns that the
asymptotic assumptions fail.  westata reports ``0`` instead, with the same
``p = 1``.  The reason is that a pseudo-inverse routinely produces a
quadratic form on the order of ``-1e-18`` through pure round-off: keeping
the sign would turn floating-point noise into a "genuinely negative
statistic" every time the difference matrix is near-singular, which is a
worse failure mode than reporting the floor.  ``df``, ``p`` and the warning
all still match Stata; only the sign of an uninterpretable statistic
differs.
exports.signature: (consistent: 'Any', efficient: 'Any', *, constant: 'bool' = False, sigmamore: 'bool' = False, sigmaless: 'bool' = False) -> 'HausmanResult'

exports.name: im_pesaran_shin
exports.docstring:
Im-Pesaran-Shin panel unit-root test.

Parameters
----------
trend:
    Include a linear trend in each panel's ADF regression (Stata ``trend``).
demean:
    Remove the cross-sectional mean before running the per-panel regressions
    (Stata ``demean``), which is the IPS test with cross-sectional means removed.
lags:
    Number of lagged differences. ``None`` reproduces Stata's default of none.

exports.name: kpss
exports.docstring:
KPSS test for stationarity, as ``kpss varname``.

``trend=True`` is Stata's DEFAULT (``trend stationary``); pass ``trend=False`` for its
``notrend`` option. ``maxlag=None`` uses KPSS's rule, ``int(4*(n/100)**0.25)``. Supplying
``maxlag`` explicitly also changes the printed Maxlag line, because Stata only says "chosen by
Schwert criterion" for the automatic choice.

``name`` is optional: Stata prints the variable name in the title and H0 line, but a bare
ndarray has no name, so the generic wording is kept when it is omitted.
exports.signature: (values: 'Any', *, trend: 'bool' = True, maxlag: 'int | None' = None, name: 'str' = '') -> 'KpssResult'

exports.name: levin_lin_chu
exports.docstring:
Levin-Lin-Chu panel unit-root test.

``constant`` and ``trend`` choose the deterministic specification, matching Stata's
``noconstant`` and ``trend`` options: neither gives model 1, constant only model 2 (the
default), both model 3.
exports.signature: (data: 'pd.DataFrame', *, variable: 'str', entity: 'str', time: 'str', trend: 'bool' = False, constant: 'bool' = True, demean: 'bool' = False, lags: 'int | None' = None, hac_lags: 'int | None' = None) -> 'LlcResult'

exports.name: lincom_as_stata
exports.docstring:
Evaluate one linear combination (Stata ``lincom``).

Stata moves a bare constant to the right-hand side of the printed
constraint and leaves the variance untouched, so
``lincom 2*weight - 3*foreign + 10`` reports ``14.9369115`` with the same
``se = 3.2272271`` as ``lincom 2*weight - 3*foreign`` reports for
``4.9369115``.  The constant is added to the estimate and never enters
:math:`L V L'`.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', expression: 'str', *, level: 'float' = 0.95, eform: 'bool' = False) -> 'Any'

exports.name: linktest
exports.docstring:
Stata's ``linktest``.

Parameters
----------
result:
    A fitted result whose linear index is a single ``xb``.

Raises
------
NotImplementedError
    For an estimator ``linktest.ado:52-66`` refuses, or one this package cannot
    refit.
ValueError
    When the estimation data was not retained, or the refit cannot produce a
    ``_hatsq`` coefficient.

Notes
-----
The test is two-sided against a t distribution with the REFIT's residual degrees of
freedom -- ``linktest.ado:132`` reads ``e(df_r)`` after the refit, not before.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any') -> 'LinkTestResult'

exports.name: lrtest
exports.docstring:
Likelihood-ratio test that ``restricted`` is adequate (``[R] lrtest``).

Parameters
----------
unrestricted:
    The model with the larger parameter set.
restricted:
    The model with fewer parameters.  Stata only checks the parameter
    *counts*; the coefficient names are compared here too, but a mismatch is
    reported as a warning rather than a refusal, because Stata computes the
    statistic anyway (and the LR is then usually negative, which is exactly
    what a non-nested pair deserves).

Raises
------
ConsistencyError
    The models were fit on different samples, the two parameter counts are
    equal (Stata ``r(498)``: ``df(unrestricted) = df(restricted)``), or a
    log-likelihood is unavailable.

Warns
-----
RuntimeWarning
    ``unrestricted`` has a lower log-likelihood than ``restricted``, which
    cannot happen for a genuinely nested pair.  The statistic is still
    computed (and is negative) rather than silently reported as 0, matching
    Stata's ``LR chi2(1) = -2.6835`` output.
RuntimeWarning
    ``restricted`` estimates a coefficient ``unrestricted`` does not, so the
    pair is not nested even though the counts differ.  Stata would compute
    the (negative) statistic regardless; so does this, with a warning.
exports.signature: (unrestricted: 'Any', restricted: 'Any') -> 'LRTestResult'

exports.name: margins
exports.docstring:
Compute marginal effects or predictive margins.

Parameters
----------
dydx:
    Name(s) of the covariates to differentiate with respect to.  Omit to
    get adjusted predictions (``margins`` without ``dydx()``).
at:
    ``{"z": 1}`` fixes covariates at the given values before averaging.
over:
    Column name (or index array) defining groups to report separately.

    The design matrix and its column names.  If omitted, the estimator must
    have stored them; otherwise a clear error is raised.

    change* for these (prediction at 1 minus prediction at 0) rather than a
    derivative; passing them switches to that definition.
outcome:
    Ordered models only: the category whose probability ``predict, pr``
    refers to (Stata's ``predict, pr outcome(#k)``).  ``None`` is Stata's
    default, category 1.

exports.name: nlcom
exports.docstring:
Point estimate, standard error and interval for ``g(b)``.

Parameters
----------
result:
    Any estimation result exposing ``params``, ``param_names`` and
    ``cov_params()`` (every westata estimator does).
expression:
    A function of the coefficients written with ``_b[name]``, e.g.
    ``"exp(_b[x1])"``, ``"_b[x1] / _b[x2]"`` or ``"_b[x1] + _b[x2]"``.

    Confidence level as a fraction (Stata's ``level(95)`` is ``0.95``).

    interval, exactly as :func:`run_lincom` does for ``lincom, eform``.

LincomResult

    special case.  Inference follows the model's distribution (``t`` with
    ``e(df_r)``, or the normal for a ``z`` model); see the module docstring
    for the known deviation from Stata's printed ``z``.

form Stata allows at top level (``or=(exp(_b[mpg]))``, ``_b[x1]``), which is what the
manual's later examples use.
exports.signature: (text: 'str') -> 'ParsedExpressionList'

exports.name: pperron
exports.docstring:
Phillips-Perron test, spelled the way Stata spells it.

``pperron(y, trend=True)`` is ``unitroot(y, test="pp", regression="ct")``; the option mapping
is the same as :func:`dfuller`.
exports.signature: (endog: 'Any', *, trend: 'bool' = False, lags: 'int | None' = None, autolag: 'str | None' = None, regression: 'str | None' = None) -> 'UnitRootResult'

exports.name: prais
exports.docstring:
Fit a Prais-Winsten AR(1) regression, as Stata's ``prais``.

Thin wrapper over :class:`westata.Prais` -- the class is the implementation; this
function keeps the documented ``(data, formula, *, ...)`` call working (R2.7).
exports.signature: (data: 'pd.DataFrame', formula: 'str', *, maxiter: 'int' = 100, tolerance: 'float' = 1e-06, corc: 'bool' = False) -> 'PraisResult'

exports.name: prais_winsten
exports.docstring:
Iterated Prais-Winsten / Cochrane-Orcutt estimate.

Returns ``(coefficients, rho, iterations, trace)``. ``rho`` may be given to run a single pass
instead of iterating; the trace is then empty.

``trace`` is the sequence Stata prints as its iteration log, as ``(iteration, rho)`` pairs with
``Iteration 0`` a literal zero. Reproducing it needs the ado's PASS ORDER, not only its
arithmetic (``prais.ado:172-217``)::

    lastrho = 2 ; rho = 0
    while abs(rho - lastrho) > tol {
        lastrho = rho
        resid = y - X b        <- residual of the PREVIOUS fit (plain OLS on pass 1)
        rho   = crcar1(resid)  <- the value that gets printed
        b     = fit AT rho     <- and the value the next pass fits with
    }

``rho`` is the loop variable and the fit input; the coefficients follow it. Re-seeding ``rho``
from the OLS estimate, or treating the fit and the estimate as one unit, produces
``0.3895, 0.3975, ...`` where Stata has ``0.4008, 0.4009, ...``.

Two further conditions are satisfied elsewhere: ``_rho_from_residuals`` is the slope of the
residual on its own lag with no constant (``_crcar1.ado:37-42``), and ``_transform_corc`` drops
the first row (``prais_e.ado:28-33``).
exports.signature: (exog: 'np.ndarray', endog: 'np.ndarray', *, maxiter: 'int' = 100, tolerance: 'float' = 1e-06, rho: 'float | None' = None, corc: 'bool' = False) -> 'tuple[np.ndarray, float, int, list[tuple[int, float]]]'

exports.name: predict
exports.docstring:
Return a prediction of the requested ``kind`` for ``exog``.

Parameters
----------
exog:
    Design matrix to predict at.  Pass the estimation sample for the usual
    in-sample predictions, or new rows for out-of-sample work.
kind:
    One of the types returned by :func:`supported_types`.  ``"stdp"`` and
    ``"stdf"`` are the prediction standard errors (``[R] predict``): the
    standard error of the linear prediction, and of the forecast, which adds
    the residual variance.

    When ``None`` the type follows Stata's per-model default
    (:func:`default_predict_kind`): ``xb`` for linear models, ``pr`` for
    logit/probit/ordinal, ``n`` for count models.  It used to default to ``xb``
    everywhere, which made a bare ``res.predict()`` return log-odds on a logit --
    neither Stata's meaning nor statsmodels'.
lower, upper:
    Censoring limits, required by the ``tobit`` types ``e`` and ``ystar``.
    When omitted, ``result.e["llopt"]``/``result.e["ulopt"]`` are used (the older
    ``lower``/``upper`` spelling is still honoured as a fallback).
outcome:
    Ordered models only: which category's probability ``pr`` returns
    (Stata's ``predict, pr outcome(#k)``).  ``None`` means Stata's default,
    category 1.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', exog: 'np.ndarray', kind: 'str | None' = None, *, lower: 'float | None' = None, upper: 'float | None' = None, outcome: 'int | None' = None, n: 'int | float | None' = None) -> 'np.ndarray'

exports.name: pwcompare
exports.docstring:
All pairwise differences between the levels of a factor variable.

Row ``(i, j)`` with ``j > i`` reports ``level_j - level_i``, so a factor with
``L`` levels yields ``L * (L - 1) / 2`` rows in that order.

Parameters
----------
result, term, level:
    As in :func:`contrast`.
adjust:
    Multiple-comparison adjustment.  Only ``None`` (Stata's ``adjust(none)``,
    also accepted spelled out) is implemented: every real correction raises
    :class:`UnsupportedError` rather than being silently dropped.

Returns
-------
list[LincomResult]
    ``L * (L - 1) / 2`` comparisons.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', term: 'str', *, level: 'float' = 0.95, adjust: 'str | None' = None) -> 'Any'

exports.name: rcm
exports.docstring:
Regression control method for one treated unit.

``response``/``predictors``/``unit``/``time`` are equal-length sequences describing a
balanced panel: the outcome, the candidate control variables, the unit identifier and the
period. ``treated_unit`` names the unit receiving treatment at ``treatment_period``.

``selected`` may name the control units to use directly (this reproduces Stata exactly when
the same set is chosen). Left as ``None``, a forward search is run on the pre-period by the
``criterion``.
exports.signature: (response: 'Any', predictors: 'Any', unit: 'Any', time: 'Any', *, treated_unit: 'Any', treatment_period: 'float', method: 'str' = 'forward', criterion: 'str' = 'aicc', selected: 'Sequence[Any] | None' = None, max_predictors: 'int | None' = None) -> 'RcmResult'

exports.name: rdrobust
exports.docstring:
Sharp RD estimate at ``cutoff``.

Bandwidth selection is not implemented: pass ``bandwidth`` explicitly, or the default
``None`` raises rather than silently choosing one. Stata's MSE-optimal selector is a
separate, considerably larger piece of work.
exports.signature: (response: 'Any', running: 'Any', *, cutoff: 'float' = 0.0, bandwidth: 'float | None' = None, bias_bandwidth: 'float | None' = None, order: 'int' = 1, bias_order: 'int' = 2, kernel: 'str' = 'triangular', covs: 'Any' = None) -> 'RdRobustResult'

exports.name: render_estimates_table
exports.docstring:
Reproduce ``estimates table m1 m2 ..., b se``.

``model_names`` is the equivalent of the ``estimates store`` names: Stata prints whatever the
models were stored as, abbreviated to ten characters where needed.

``star`` is Stata's ``star(...)``: a descending triple of p-value thresholds. Passing it changes
the LAYOUT, not just the cells -- see the measurement notes in the body.

``pvalues`` adds Stata's ``p`` row under each coefficient -- four decimal places WITH the
leading zero, unlike the coefficient itself. ``estimates table ..., b p`` and ``..., p`` are the
same thing (``b`` is always printed), and ``p`` cannot be combined with ``star(...)``: Stata
rejects that pair.

``mtitle`` selects the **``esttab`` shape** instead of the ``estimates table`` one: a header with
``(1) (2) ...`` numbers and the model names, no ``Variable |`` gutter, a ``12 + 16*n`` rule and
three-significant-figure coefficients. ``stats`` adds the footer rows that ``esttab`` prints for
names such as ``"N"``, ``"r2"``, ``"r2_a"`` and ``"rmse"``.
exports.signature: (results: 'Sequence[Any]', *, model_names: 'Sequence[str] | None' = None, se: 'bool' = True, star: 'Sequence[float] | None' = None, mtitle: 'bool' = False, stats: 'Sequence[str] | None' = None, pvalues: 'bool' = False) -> 'str'

exports.name: render_esttab
exports.docstring: Render ``results`` as Stata's ``esttab`` prints them.
exports.signature: (results: 'Sequence[Any]', *, model_names: 'Sequence[str] | None', digits: 'int' = 3, se: 'bool' = True, stars: 'bool' = True, stats: 'Sequence[tuple[str, Any]] | None' = None, stats_digits: 'int' = 3) -> 'str'

exports.name: suest
exports.docstring:
Stata's ``suest`` -- stack several fits into one simultaneous covariance.

Parameters
----------
models:
    Two or more fitted linear results, all on the SAME observations.
names:
    Labels for each model; defaults to ``model1``, ``model2``, ...
cluster:
    Cluster labels, giving Stata's ``vce(cluster clustvar)`` form
    (``suest.sthlp:108-109``).  Each observation's stacked score is summed within its
    cluster before the outer product, so the covariance reflects within-cluster
    dependence.

Raises
------
NotImplementedError
    When a model cannot produce scores -- a non-linear estimator whose score is not
    the residual, or one without a design matrix.
ValueError
    When fewer than two models are given, when their sample sizes differ, when a
    block is singular, or when the cluster labels do not match the sample.

Notes
-----
``suest.sthlp:105-107`` advises estimating the components WITHOUT
``vce(robust)``/``vce(cluster)``: ``suest`` supplies the robust VCE itself, so a
robust component would be doubly corrected. The sandwich built here uses only the
residuals and the design, so it is robust regardless of what the components used --
which is exactly why the advice exists.
exports.signature: (models: 'Sequence[Any]', *, names: 'Sequence[str] | None' = None, cluster: 'Any' = None) -> 'SucestResult'

exports.name: summarize
exports.docstring:
Stata's ``summarize`` over ``data`` (a DataFrame, Series or array).

``variables`` names the columns to report; omitted, every column is included. Missing
values are excluded per variable, exactly as Stata's ``Obs`` column reports the number of
non-missing observations.
exports.signature: (data: 'Any', variables: 'Sequence[str] | None' = None, *, weights: 'Any' = None, detail: 'bool' = False) -> 'Any'

exports.name: supported_types
exports.docstring: Return the predict types available for ``model_name``.
exports.signature: (model_name: 'str') -> 'tuple[str, ...]'

exports.name: synth
exports.docstring:
Fit a synthetic control (Stata ``synth``), extended feature set.

Implements Stata's default path plus ``unitnames()``, per-predictor
``var(period)`` windows, ``keep()``, the four optimiser settings and an
algorithm-equivalent ``nested`` / ``allopt`` outer V search.  Graphics and
``synth2``'s placebo/LOO remain out of scope.

Evidence grading is per quantity and MEASURED, never assumed: see
``tests/conformance/registry.yml``.  ``nested``/``allopt`` and RMSPE cannot
be bit-identical to Stata (closed-source ``ml`` optimiser + rank-deficient
QP + non-deterministic C++ plugin); they are E2 by construction.
exports.signature: (data: 'Any', *, unit: 'str', time: 'str', depvar: 'str', predictors: 'Sequence[str]', trunit: 'Any', trperiod: 'float', counit: 'Sequence[Any] | None' = None, xperiod: 'Sequence[float] | None' = None, mspeperiod: 'Sequence[float] | None' = None, resultsperiod: 'Sequence[float] | None' = None, customV: 'Sequence[float] | None' = None, unitnames: 'str | None' = None, margin: 'float' = 0.005, maxiter: 'int' = 1000, sigf: 'int' = 12, bound: 'float' = 10, nested: 'bool' = False, allopt: 'bool' = False, technique: 'str | None' = None, iterate: 'int | None' = None, nrtolerance: 'float | None' = None, nonrtolerance: 'bool' = False, difficult: 'bool' = False, search: 'str | None' = None, trace: 'bool' = False, keep: 'str | None' = None, replace: 'bool' = False, figure: 'bool' = False, placebo: 'bool' = False, **unsupported: 'Any') -> 'SynthResult'

exports.name: synth2
exports.docstring:
Fit Stata ``synth2``'s NON-GRAPHICS feature set.

All optimisation is delegated to :func:`westata.synth`.  See the module
docstring and ``docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-11-synth2-design.md`` for
the per-quantity evidence grading and the exact ado formulas.
exports.signature: (data: 'Any', *, unit: 'str', time: 'str', depvar: 'str', predictors: 'Sequence[str]', trunit: 'Any', trperiod: 'float', counit: 'Sequence[Any] | None' = None, ctrlunit: 'Sequence[Any] | None' = None, preperiod: 'Sequence[float] | None' = None, postperiod: 'Sequence[float] | None' = None, xperiod: 'Sequence[float] | None' = None, mspeperiod: 'Sequence[float] | None' = None, customV: 'Sequence[float] | None' = None, nested: 'bool' = False, allopt: 'bool' = False, margin: 'float' = 0.005, maxiter: 'int' = 1000, sigf: 'int' = 12, bound: 'float' = 10, placebo: 'str | None' = None, loo: 'bool' = False, figure: 'bool' = False, nofigure: 'bool' = False, savegraph: 'str | None' = None, symbol: 'int' = 1, frame: 'str | None' = None, show: 'int | None' = None, **unsupported: 'Any') -> 'Synth2Result'

exports.name: tebalance_summarize
exports.docstring:
Balance table comparing raw and matched means/variances.

``covariates`` is an ``(n, k)`` array; ``match_weights`` holds the control-side matching
weights (one per observation, zero for untreated controls that were never used, and zero
for all treated rows). ``names`` labels the columns.
exports.signature: (treatment: 'Any', covariates: 'Any', *, match_weights: 'Any' = None, names: 'list[str] | None' = None, exact: 'tuple[str, ...]' = (), normalize_counts: 'bool' = False) -> 'BalanceSummary'

exports.name: teffects_nnmatch
exports.docstring:
ATET by Mahalanobis-distance nearest-neighbour matching.

``caliper`` caps the distance a match may have; ``None`` means no cap (Stata's default).
``tie_tolerance`` is the absolute distance within which two controls count as equally near.
exports.signature: (response: 'Any', treatment: 'Any', covariates: 'Any', *, nneighbor: 'int' = 1, caliper: 'float | None' = None, tie_tolerance: 'float' = 1e-10) -> 'NnmatchResult'

exports.name: teffects_psmatch
exports.docstring:
ATET by propensity-score matching, as ``teffects psmatch ..., atet``.

``covariates`` is an ``(n, k)`` array. The propensity score comes from a logit of
``treatment`` on those covariates with an intercept, which is what Stata's treatment
model does by default (verified: the logit coefficients agree to 1e-7).

``nneighbor`` is Stata's ``nn()``; ties at the k-th smallest distance are ALL included,
so the realised number of matches can exceed it.

``tie_tolerance`` is the absolute propensity-score difference still counted as a tie. It
must be TIGHT. The old 1e-6 default lumped two controls 0.0011575908 and 0.00115824
apart -- a difference of 6e-7 -- into one tie for treated unit 2, which reported four
matches where Stata uses three. Measured across nn(1) to nn(5) on nsw_dw::

    tolerance   matches Stata
    1e-6        4 of 5      (nn(3) gives 2412.8207 against 2397.636)
    1e-9        5 of 5
    1e-12       5 of 5
    0           5 of 5

1e-9 separates distinct distances while still absorbing the logit's own numerical noise,
which is far below that scale.

``caliper`` is Stata's ``caliper(#)``: a control further than # in propensity-score
distance is ineligible, and a treated unit with nothing inside the caliper is dropped
from the estimate (Stata reports those as "no matches"). ``None`` means no cap, which is
the default.

The AI-robust standard error is NOT computed (see the module docstring), so the
inferential fields stay NaN.
exports.signature: (response: 'Any', treatment: 'Any', covariates: 'Any', *, nneighbor: 'int' = 1, tie_tolerance: 'float' = 1e-09, outcome: 'str' = '', caliper: 'float | None' = None) -> 'PsmatchResult'

exports.name: teffects_ra
exports.docstring:
Regression-adjustment treatment effect, as ``teffects ra (y x) (t)``.

``covariates`` is an ``(n, k)`` array; a constant column is prepended unless
``add_constant`` is False.
exports.signature: (response: 'Any', treatment: 'Any', covariates: 'Any', *, estimand: 'str' = 'ate', add_constant: 'bool' = True) -> 'TefectsRaResult'

exports.name: test_as_stata
exports.docstring:
Wald test of one or more linear hypotheses.

Parameters
----------
*specs:
    Each argument is a Stata-style hypothesis.  A bare coefficient list
    (``"x1 x2"``) tests that all are zero; an equality chain (``"x1 = x2"``)
    tests that difference.  Multiple specs are tested jointly.
coef:
    Stata's ``coef`` option: also return the constrained estimates
    ``b_c = b - V R'(RVR')^-1(Rb - r)`` and ``V_c = V - VR'(RVR')^-1 RV``.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', *specs: 'Any', coef: 'bool' = False) -> 'WaldTest | dict[str, Any]'

exports.name: testnl
exports.docstring:
Wald test of one or more nonlinear constraints (Stata ``testnl``).

``expression`` holds one constraint (``"exp(_b[x1]) = 2"``) or several
separated by commas or whitespace, which are tested jointly.  A bare
expression is tested against zero.  The reference distribution is
``chi2(q)`` with ``q`` the number of constraints, as ``[R] testnl`` reports.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', expression: 'str') -> 'WaldTest'

exports.name: unitroot
exports.docstring:
Unit-root test (Stata ``dfuller`` / ``pperron`` / ``kpss``).

Parameters
----------
test:
    ``"adf"`` (``dfuller``), ``"pp"`` (``pperron``) or ``"kpss"``.
regression:
    Deterministic terms: ``"c"``, ``"n"``, ``"ct"``, ``"ctt"``.
autolag:
    Lag selection for ``"adf"``. ``None`` (the default) means "use exactly
    ``maxlag`` lags", which is Stata's behaviour: ``dfuller`` uses ``lags(0)``
    unless asked otherwise. A criterion name selects the lag the statsmodels
    way, which is a DIFFERENT test from Stata's default -- on macro_swatson's
    ``inf`` column, AIC selection reported -2.571 against Stata's -3.718.

Notes
-----
For ``"adf"`` the *statistic* and the MacKinnon p-value are the same test
Stata runs and agree to ~1e-13, but the printed **critical values** are not
MacKinnon response-surface values: ``dfuller.ado`` interpolates a six-point
table linearly in N.  This function returns that table's values, so a user
comparing the printed band sees the same numbers Stata prints.  The p-value
is unaffected and remains the MacKinnon one.
exports.signature: (endog: 'Any', *, test: 'str' = 'adf', regression: 'str' = 'c', maxlag: 'int | None' = None, autolag: 'str | None' = None) -> 'UnitRootResult'

exports.name: vargranger
exports.docstring:
Build the ``vargranger`` table for a fitted ``VARResults``.

Stata's ``vargranger`` refuses anything but a var/svar/ivsvar/xtvar estimate::

    vargranger only works with estimates from var, svar, ivsvar,or xtvar

A VECM is not among them. Passing one must say so rather than surface an AttributeError from
the missing ``granger_causality``, which names neither the test nor the reason.
exports.signature: (fitted: 'Any') -> 'VarGrangerResult'

exports.name: varlmar
exports.docstring:
LM test for residual autocorrelation at each of lags ``1..mlag``.

``result`` must be a fitted VAR (or a VECM, whose residuals are the same object) exposing
the residuals, the lag order and the original data.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', *, mlag: 'int' = 2) -> 'LmarResult'

exports.name: varsoc
exports.docstring:
Lag-order selection, as Stata's ``varsoc``.

``data`` holds the endogenous series in time order (rows) by equation (columns). Missing
rows must already be dropped. ``trend="c"`` fits a constant, which is Stata's default.
exports.signature: (data: 'np.ndarray | pd.DataFrame', *, maxlag: 'int' = 4, trend: 'str' = 'c', names: 'list[str] | None' = None) -> 'VarSocResult'

exports.name: varstable
exports.docstring:
Eigenvalues of the VAR's companion matrix, as ``varstable``.

``result`` must be a fitted VAR exposing ``coefs`` with shape ``(lags, K, K)``.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any') -> 'VarStableResult'

exports.name: varwle
exports.docstring:
Wald lag-exclusion tests, as ``varwle``.

``result`` must be a fitted VAR exposing the Stata-ordered parameter vector and its
covariance (``stata_params`` / ``stata_cov_params``). Using the backend's own ordering
would silently test the wrong coefficients.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any') -> 'VarWleResult'

exports.name: veclmar
exports.docstring:
VECM residual autocorrelation test, as ``veclmar``.

``veclmar.ado`` converts the VECM to its VAR form with ``_vec_postvar`` and forwards to
``varlmar``. That conversion is NOT the identity: ``_vec_postvar.ado:70-71`` calls
``_vecmkce``, which materialises the cointegrating term ``beta'Y_{t-1}`` as an extra
regressor. The equivalent VAR therefore has

    Delta Y_t = c + alpha (beta'Y_{t-1}) + Gamma Delta Y_{t-1} + e_t

with the error-correction term as a COLUMN, rather than the unrestricted VAR's own lags of
the levels. Using the unrestricted VAR regressors gave 14.8557 / 12.5931 against Stata's
8.8911 / 4.8537 -- wrong at both orders, and in the same way ``varlmar``'s accumulation bug
was wrong.

Verified against ``vec dinf unem, lags(2) rank(1)`` then ``veclmar`` on macro_swatson.dta:

    lag 1: chi2 8.8911  df 4  p 0.06388
    lag 2: chi2 4.8537  df 4  p 0.30264
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', *, mlag: 'int' = 2) -> 'LmarResult'

exports.name: vecrank
exports.docstring:
Johansen cointegration rank test, as ``vecrank``.

``data`` holds the endogenous series in time order (rows) by equation (columns); missing
rows must already be dropped. ``lags`` counts the VAR lag order as Stata does, so the
number of differenced lags is ``lags - 1``.

``show_max=True`` is Stata's ``max`` option: the trace table is printed with a SECOND table of
maximum-eigenvalue statistics below it. Stata always shows both when ``max`` is given, so this
is a display flag -- the ``maximum`` and ``maximum_critical`` fields are populated either way.
exports.signature: (data: 'Any', *, lags: 'int' = 2, trend: 'str' = 'constant', show_max: 'bool' = False) -> 'VecRankResult'

exports.name: vecstable
exports.docstring:
Eigenvalues of the VECM's companion matrix, as ``vecstable``.

``result`` must be a fitted VECM exposing ``alpha``, ``beta`` and ``gamma``, with
``neqs`` equations and at least one lag order.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any') -> 'VecStableResult'

exports.name: wntestq
exports.docstring:
Ljung-Box Q, as ``wntestq``.

``corrgram.ado:68`` builds it as

.. math:: Q = n(n+2) \sum_{k=1}^{p} \hat\rho_k^2 / (n-k)

``wntestq.ado:16-24`` takes the default lag count from ``ac``, so it is
``max(1, min(int(n/2) - 2, 40))`` -- measured: 30 observations give ``chi2(13)``, and
758 give ``chi2(40)`` rather than the 377 an ``(n-k)//2`` rule would claim. Measured
numbers: Q 26.1974, p .0160; with ``lags(10)``: Q 16.3718, p .0895.

``time`` stands in for ``tsset``; see :func:`estat_dwatson`.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', *, lags: 'int | None' = None, time: 'str | Any | None' = None, delta: 'float' = 1.0) -> 'PortmanteauResult'

exports.name: xttest0
exports.docstring:
Breusch-Pagan LM test for a random effect, as ``xttest0`` after ``xtreg, re``.

``entity`` supplies the group labels when ``result`` does not carry them. The residuals
are always those of the POOLED OLS regression, which is what the test is built on --
Stata takes them from the ``re`` fit's ``e(rss)`` scale but the statistic itself uses the
pooled residuals.
exports.signature: (result: 'Any', *, entity: 'Any' = None) -> 'XtTest0Result'

methods.name: conf_int
methods.docstring:
Confidence intervals for the coefficients.

Uses the Student-t reference distribution for ``dist="t"`` and the
standard normal for ``dist="z"``.

``alpha`` defaults to ``1 - level``: a result estimated with Stata's
``level(90)`` reports 90% intervals unless a caller asks for something else
explicitly. Hard-coding 0.05 here was what made ``level(#)`` unrepresentable --
the model could not influence the interval even if it recorded a level.

methods.name: contrast
methods.docstring: ANOVA-style contrast of a factor's levels (Stata `contrast`).

methods.name: cov_params
methods.docstring: Return the covariance matrix of the parameter estimates.

methods.name: ereturn_list
methods.docstring:
Stata's ``ereturn list`` -- the four sections of one estimation result.

Captured from a live ``quietly regress lnw s expr`` then ``ereturn list`` (round 249):

    (blank)
    scalars:
                      e(N) =  758
                   e(df_m) =  2
                      e(F) =  160.164773596988
    (blank)
    macros:
                e(cmdline) : "regress lnw s expr"
                  e(title) : "Linear regression"
    (blank)
    matrices:
                      e(b) :  1 x 3
                      e(V) :  3 x 3
    (blank)
    functions:
                 e(sample)

The three column shapes differ: a scalar is ``<name> = <value>`` with the name
RIGHT-aligned to column 21; a macro is ``<name> : "<text>"`` with the name right-aligned
to 21 and the text in double quotes; a matrix is ``<name> :  <r> x <c>`` with TWO spaces
after the colon (Stata pads to align the dimensions); a function is just the name.
The whole block opens with a blank line, like every other Stata output block.

methods.name: estat_auc
methods.docstring:
Stata's ``estat auc`` -- the area under the ROC curve.

``logit_estat.ado:19-21`` dispatches the subcommand to ``lroc, nograph``.

methods.name: estat_bgodfrey
methods.signature: (self, *, lags: 'int | Sequence[int]' = 1, nomiss0: 'bool' = False, time: 'str | Sequence[Any] | None' = None, delta: 'float' = 1.0) -> 'Any'
methods.docstring:
Stata's ``estat bgodfrey`` -- the Breusch-Godfrey LM test for autocorrelation.

The implementation has existed in ``westata.postestimation.bgodfrey`` since round 191
but was only reachable as ``ws.estat_bgodfrey(result)``; ``estat dwatson`` got its
wiring in round 93 and this one was left behind, so the two serial-correlation
commands had different surfaces. Pass ``time=`` for the ``tsset`` axis and
``lags=``/``nomiss0=`` as in Stata.

methods.name: estat_classification
methods.docstring: Stata's ``estat classification`` -- the 2x2 classification table.

methods.name: estat_corrgram
methods.signature: (self, *, lags: 'int | None' = None, time: 'str | Any | None' = None, delta: 'float' = 1.0) -> 'Any'
methods.docstring:
Stata's ``corrgram`` -- autocorrelations, partial autocorrelations and Q.

Stata spells it ``corrgram`` rather than ``estat corrgram``; the method name follows
the ``estat_``-prefixed convention the rest of this object uses so that
``ws.estat_corrgram(...)`` and ``result.estat_corrgram()`` stay symmetrical.

methods.name: estat_dwatson
methods.docstring:
Stata's ``estat dwatson`` -- the Durbin-Watson d statistic.

``westata.postestimation.serial.estat_dwatson`` has existed and matched Stata for some
time, but it was never reachable from a fitted result: the report's chapter 7-9 checks
call ``result.estat_dwatson()`` and got AttributeError. The implementation was correct,
the wiring was missing.

Pass ``time=`` to make the differences follow a ``tsset`` axis; without it they follow
the row order, which is only the same thing when the sample has no gaps.

methods.name: estat_endogenous
methods.docstring: Stata's ``estat endogenous`` -- Durbin-Wu endogeneity test.

methods.name: estat_esize
methods.docstring:
Stata's ``estat esize`` -- eta/epsilon/omega-squared effect sizes.

``regress_postestimation.sthlp:599-614`` restricts it to linear models; eta-squared
is ``R^2`` and carries a noncentral-F interval.

methods.name: estat_firststage
methods.docstring:
Stata's ``estat firststage`` -- IV first-stage diagnostics.

Reports each endogenous regressor's first-stage R-squared, adjusted
R-squared, partial R-squared and the joint F of the excluded
instruments; with more than one endogenous regressor it adds Shea's
partial R-squared.

methods.name: estat_gof
methods.signature: (self, *, y: 'Any' = None, mu: 'Any' = None, group: 'int | None' = None) -> 'Any'
methods.docstring:
Stata's ``estat gof`` -- Poisson goodness-of-fit tests.

Only defined for ``poisson``: Stata has no ``estat gof`` after ``nbreg``
(``nbreg`` sets no ``e(estat_cmd)``), so requesting it there raises
``NotImplementedError`` rather than returning an invented statistic.

methods.name: estat_hettest
methods.signature: (self, *, method: 'str' = 'normal', variables: 'Sequence[str] | None' = None, rhs: 'bool' = False, mtest: 'str | None' = None) -> 'Any'
methods.docstring:
Stata's ``estat hettest`` -- Breusch-Pagan / Cook-Weisberg.

With no ``variables`` the auxiliary regression is on the FITTED VALUES,
which is Stata's no-varlist behaviour; ``rhs=True`` uses every regressor.
Refuses, like Stata, after a robust or clustered VCE, on pweighted data
and after a ``noconstant`` fit.

methods.name: estat_ic
methods.signature: (self, *, n: 'float | None' = None, df: 'float | None' = None) -> 'Any'
methods.docstring:
Stata's ``estat ic`` -- AIC, BIC, AICc and CAIC.

``df`` defaults to ``rank(V)``, matching ``estimates.ado:977-978``; ``N``
is ``e(N_ic)`` when recorded and ``e(N)`` otherwise.

methods.name: estat_imtest
methods.docstring: Stata's ``estat imtest`` -- Cameron & Trivedi's IM-test.

methods.name: estat_moran
methods.docstring:
Stata's ``estat moran`` -- Moran's test for spatial correlation in residuals.

Requires a spatial weighting matrix.  This package has no ``spmatrix`` toolchain,
so the matrix is passed explicitly; see
:mod:`westata.postestimation.moran` for the caveat about Stata's own statistic.

methods.name: estat_mundlak
methods.signature: (self, *, storer: 'Any' = None, entity: 'str | None' = None, time: 'str | None' = None) -> 'Any'
methods.docstring:
Stata's ``estat mundlak`` -- the Mundlak panel specification test.

Adds the within-group means of the regressors to the random-effects equation and
tests them jointly to zero: ``xtreg_postestimation.sthlp:366-370``.  A rejection
means the unobserved effect is correlated with ``x``, so the random-effects
estimator is inconsistent.

methods.name: estat_overid
methods.docstring:
Stata's ``estat overid`` -- overidentification restrictions test.

Reports Sargan (with Basmann's finite-sample variant) for 2SLS/LIML and
Hansen's J for GMM.

methods.name: estat_ovtest
methods.docstring: Stata's ``estat ovtest`` -- Ramsey RESET test for omitted variables.

methods.name: estat_ptrends
methods.docstring:
Stata's ``estat ptrends`` -- the parallel-trends test for DiD.

Only defined after ``didregress``/``xtdidregress``; see
:func:`westata.estimators.did.estat_ptrends`.

methods.name: estat_summarize
methods.signature: (self, *, data: 'pd.DataFrame | None' = None, variables: 'Sequence[str] | None' = None, weights: 'Any' = None, weight_type: 'str | None' = None, cluster: 'Any' = None, cluster_name: 'str' = '', noweights: 'bool' = False, noheader: 'bool' = False, labels: 'Mapping[str, str] | None' = None) -> 'Any'
methods.docstring: Stata's ``estat summarize`` -- describe the estimation sample.

methods.name: estat_szroeter
methods.signature: (self, variables: 'Sequence[str] | None' = None, *, rhs: 'bool' = False, mtest: 'str | None' = None) -> 'Any'
methods.docstring:
Stata's ``estat szroeter`` -- Szroeter's rank test for heteroskedasticity.

Refuses, like ``szroeter.ado:13-22``, after anything other than ``regress``, and
on weighted or clustered fits.

methods.name: estat_vce
methods.docstring:
Stata's ``estat vce`` -- print the coefficient covariance matrix.

``correlation=True`` gives ``estat vce, correlation``.  Both are pure
renderings of :meth:`cov_params`; nothing is recomputed.

Returns
-------
VceMatrix
    ``str(...)`` prints the table; ``.to_frame()`` returns the full
    symmetric matrix.

methods.name: estat_vif
methods.docstring:
Stata's ``estat vif`` -- variance inflation factors.

Only defined for linear models: the auxiliary regressions are ordinary
least squares by construction, and Stata reaches the command through
``regress_estat``.

methods.name: estat_weakrobust
methods.signature: (self, *, ar: 'bool | None' = None, clr: 'bool | None' = None, betanull: 'Any' = None) -> 'Any'
methods.docstring:
Stata's ``estat weakrobust`` -- inference robust to weak instruments.

Reports the Anderson-Rubin test, whose distribution does not depend on instrument
strength.  The conditional likelihood-ratio test (the overidentified default in
Stata) is refused with its reason; see
:func:`westata.postestimation.weakrobust.estat_weakrobust`.

methods.name: f_test
methods.docstring: statsmodels' ``f_test``: one or more restrictions reported jointly as F.

methods.name: first_stage
methods.docstring:
Stata's ``ivregress ..., first`` -- the first-stage regression table.

One block per endogenous regressor, headed "First-stage regressions": the F,
R-squared, adjusted R-squared and Root MSE of that equation, then its
coefficient table with the included exogenous variables and the excluded
instruments.

This is a different output from :meth:`estat_firststage`, which prints the
DIAGNOSTICS for the same equations. Stata offers both and they are not
substitutes, so both are here.

methods.name: get_influence
methods.docstring: Influence measures, named as statsmodels' ``OLSInfluence`` names them.

methods.name: hausman
methods.signature: (self, efficient: 'Any', *, constant: 'bool' = False, sigmamore: 'bool' = False, sigmaless: 'bool' = False) -> 'Any'
methods.docstring:
Hausman specification test (Stata `hausman`).

Keyword arguments are forwarded to
:func:`westata.postestimation.modeltests.hausman`, so the Stata
``hausman ..., constant`` option is reachable from a result object too:
``fe.hausman(re, constant=True)``.

methods.name: lincom
methods.docstring: Linear combination of parameters (Stata ``lincom``).

methods.name: linktest
methods.docstring:
Stata's ``linktest`` -- Pregibon's link test for a specification error.

Refits the same estimator with ``_hat`` and ``_hatsq`` added and reports the t
statistic of the squared term (``linktest.ado:131-132``).

methods.name: lrtest
methods.docstring: Likelihood-ratio test against a nested model (Stata `lrtest`).

methods.name: margins
methods.signature: (self, *, dydx: 'Sequence[str] | str | None' = None, eyex: 'Sequence[str] | str | None' = None, dyex: 'Sequence[str] | str | None' = None, eydx: 'Sequence[str] | str | None' = None, at: 'Mapping[str, Any] | None' = None, atmeans: 'bool' = False, over: 'str | None' = None, exog: 'np.ndarray | None' = None, param_names: 'Sequence[str] | None' = None, level: 'float' = 0.95, predict_kind: 'str | None' = None, factor_vars: 'Sequence[str] | None' = None, outcome: 'int | None' = None) -> 'Any'
methods.docstring:
Marginal effects or predictive margins (Stata ``margins``).

The design matrix is taken from :attr:`design_matrix` when the
estimator stored one; otherwise pass ``exog=`` and ``param_names=``.

methods.name: nlcom
methods.docstring: Nonlinear combination of parameters (Stata `nlcom`).

methods.name: predict
methods.signature: (self, exog: 'np.ndarray | None' = None, kind: 'str | None' = None, *, lower: 'float | None' = None, upper: 'float | None' = None, outcome: 'int | None' = None, n: 'int | float | None' = None) -> 'Any'
methods.docstring:
Typed prediction (Stata ``predict, <type>``).

Parameters
----------
exog:
    Design matrix; defaults to the stored estimation design.
kind:
    ``"xb"``, ``"pr"``, ``"n"``, ``"e"``, ``"ystar"``, ``"residuals"``,
    depending on the model.  ``None`` (the default) means "whatever Stata
    assumes", resolved by
    :func:`westata.postestimation.predict.default_predict_kind`: ``xb`` for
    linear models, ``pr`` for logit/probit/ordinal, ``n`` for count models.

    It used to default to ``"xb"`` for every estimator, so a bare
    ``logit_result.predict()`` returned log-odds -- neither Stata's meaning
    (Stata assumes ``pr`` and says so) nor statsmodels' (``sm.Logit.predict``
    returns probabilities). Pass ``kind="xb"`` for the old behaviour.

methods.name: pwcompare
methods.docstring: All pairwise level differences (Stata `pwcompare`).

methods.name: relabel_cov_type
methods.docstring:
Record the covariance type actually used, after replacing the matrix.

Needed by estimators that fit with a PLACEHOLDER covariance and then rebuild
the real one once more information is available: ``Areg`` fits with HC1 to get
the estimates, then builds the leverage-based HC2/HC3 matrix on the full dummy
design.  Before this method existed the placeholder label survived, so
``Areg(...).fit(cov_type="HC2").cov_type`` reported ``"HC1"`` while the numbers
were genuinely HC2 (measured: HC2 bse 0.069765 vs HC1 0.069568) -- a caller
labelling a table from ``.cov_type`` would have printed the wrong VCE name.

Deliberately a named method rather than a settable property: relabelling must
be an explicit act of the code that replaced the matrix, not something a caller
can do to a finished result.

methods.name: suest
methods.docstring:
Stata's ``suest`` -- stack this fit with others into one covariance.

Combines the parameter vectors and forms the simultaneous sandwich covariance
across models (``suest.sthlp:84-88``).  The models must share an estimation
sample.

methods.name: summary
methods.docstring:
Render a text summary.

Parameters
----------
style:
    ``"stata"`` (default) or ``"statsmodels"``. The default is Stata's layout because this
    package exists to reproduce it; pass ``style="statsmodels"`` for the statsmodels table.
odds_ratio:
    Exponentiate the coefficients, their standard errors and both interval
    endpoints, and relabel the column "Odds ratio" -- Stata's ``logit ..., or``.
    z and P>|z| are unaffected, since they come from the untransformed scale.
first:
    Prepend the first-stage regression, as Stata's ``ivregress ..., first`` does. Only
    available for results that expose ``first_stage()``; the block is the one that method
    already renders, which matches Stata line for line.

methods.name: t_test
methods.signature: (self, r_matrix: 'Any', cov_p: 'Any' = None, use_t: 'bool | None' = None) -> 'Any'
methods.docstring: statsmodels' ``t_test``: a single restriction reported as a t statistic.

methods.name: test
methods.docstring:
Wald test of linear hypotheses (Stata ``test``).

See :meth:`westata.postestimation.tests.run_wald_test`; this thin
forwarder exists so the results object owns its own postestimation
surface, like a Stata estimation result.

methods.name: testnl
methods.docstring: Nonlinear Wald test (Stata `testnl`).

methods.name: wald_test
methods.docstring:
statsmodels-compatible joint Wald test.

Mirrors ``statsmodels``' ``wald_test(R, q, scalar)``: returns an object with
``statistic``, ``df_denom``, ``df_num`` and ``pvalue``. When ``scalar`` is False a
chi2 test is returned instead of the F test, matching statsmodels' behaviour.

R MAY BE A CONSTRAINT STRING, as statsmodels allows: ``wald_test("s = 0")``.
statsmodels accepts a formula-like expression and so does this method -- the parsing
is delegated to :meth:`test`, which already speaks Stata's constraint syntax. Only the
return SHAPE differs: ``test`` reports Stata's F statistic with ``df``/``df_denom``,
which is what a caller of ``wald_test`` is asking for anyway.

methods.name: wntestq
methods.signature: (self, *, lags: 'int | None' = None, time: 'str | Any | None' = None, delta: 'float' = 1.0) -> 'Any'
methods.docstring: Stata's ``wntestq`` -- the Ljung-Box portmanteau Q for white noise.

properties.name: aic
properties.docstring:
AIC on the statsmodels scale: ``-2*llf + 2*k``.

``e(aic)`` stores the Gaussian-deviance form ``N log(rss/N) + 2k``, which omits the
``N(1 + log 2pi)`` constant that ``e(llf)`` carries. The two differ by exactly that
constant, and the gap grows with N -- on icecream.dta it is 85.1 (-194.37519 stored
against -109.23887 from both ``sm.OLS(...).fit().aic`` and ``estat ic``).

``result.aic`` was returning the stored number, so a caller consuming it with
statsmodels semantics got a value 85 too small while ``e["aic"]`` and ``estat_ic``
stayed self-consistent. The property now follows statsmodels (and Stata's
``estat ic``, which agree), and ``e["aic"]`` keeps the package's own convention for
anyone who reads the raw macro.

properties.name: bic
properties.docstring:
BIC on the statsmodels scale: ``-2*llf + k*log(nobs)``.

Same reasoning as :attr:`aic`: ``e(bic)`` uses the Gaussian-deviance form.

properties.name: converged
properties.docstring:
Whether the optimizer reported convergence.

``design.md:209`` lists ``converged``/``iterations``/``grad_norm`` as part of the
result surface, and Stata stores the first as ``e(converged)`` (``1`` if it
converged, ``0`` otherwise -- ``logit.sthlp:259``).  Absent means the estimator
does not run an iterative optimizer at all, which is reported as ``True`` rather
than ``False``: a closed-form fit has nothing to fail to converge.

properties.name: dist
properties.docstring: Inference distribution: ``"t"`` or ``"z"``.

properties.name: e
properties.docstring:
Stata ``e()`` scalars (item and attribute access).

Two macros are synthesised when the estimator did not record them, because
every estimation command documents both and a consumer reading ``e()``
cannot tell "not recorded" from "not applicable":

* ``e(depvar)`` falls back to ``response_name`` (``logit.sthlp:264`` and
  five other help files list "name of dependent variable");
* ``e(cmd)`` falls back to ``model_name``, which already holds Stata's
  command name (``regress``, ``logit``, ``reghdfe``, ...).

``e(cmdline)`` is deliberately NOT synthesised: it records the command as
the user TYPED it, including options, and this package has no such string.
Inventing one would be a fabricated value rather than a recovered one.

properties.name: fitted_series
properties.docstring: The fitted values with the estimation sample's index attached; see ``resid_series``.

properties.name: fvalue
properties.docstring: Model F statistic from ``e(F)``; NaN when not recorded.

properties.name: grad_norm
properties.docstring:
Norm of the gradient at the reported estimate; NaN when not recorded.

A small value is the numeric counterpart of ``converged``: the optimizer stops
when this is near zero.  It is exposed as NaN rather than ``0.0`` where the
backend does not report it, so a caller cannot mistake "unavailable" for "exactly
converged".

properties.name: iterations
properties.docstring:
Number of optimizer iterations, from ``e(ic)`` (``logit.sthlp:257``).

NaN when the estimator is not iterative or the backend did not report a count.

properties.name: level
properties.docstring: The confidence level as a FRACTION (0.95 unless ``level(#)`` was given).

properties.name: llf
properties.docstring: Log-likelihood from ``e(ll)``; NaN when not recorded.

properties.name: model
properties.docstring:
The fitted model, as statsmodels exposes it.

``statsmodels.stats.anova.anova_lm`` reads ``res.model`` and re-fits from it, so its
absence made ``anova_lm(westata_result)`` raise AttributeError. The object returned
here carries ``endog``, ``exog``, ``exog_names`` and a ``fit()`` that returns this
same result -- enough for anova_lm's contract without pretending to BE a
statsmodels model.

properties.name: odds_ratios
properties.docstring:
``exp(params)`` -- the odds ratios ``logit, or`` prints.

Only meaningful for a model whose link is log-odds; other families raise rather than
returning a number that has no interpretation. ``conf_int()`` can be exponentiated
alongside it to get Stata's odds-ratio interval.

properties.name: param_names
properties.docstring: Variable names in coefficient order.

properties.name: resid_series
properties.docstring:
The residuals with the ESTIMATION SAMPLE's index attached.

v2 report section 6 wants ``resid`` itself to be a Series, as statsmodels returns it.
Replacing the attribute would break positional access -- round 19 measured that cost on
``beta`` with a KeyError from an existing test -- so the labelled form is a separate
name, exactly as ``beta_labelled`` is.

Falls back to a default RangeIndex when the fit did not retain the observation index,
which is honest: the numbers are still there, and the index says only "row i".

properties.name: response_name
properties.docstring:
The dependent variable's name, for titles and column headings.

SOME ESTIMATORS SET THIS AS AN INSTANCE ATTRIBUTE and others do not; ARIMA and GARCH were in
the second group, so postestimation code reading it saw None. Falling back to e(depvar), which
every fit carries, gives them the same answer the formula-based estimators give.

A subclass that assigns self.response_name keeps winning, because the instance dictionary is
consulted first.

properties.name: rsquared
properties.docstring: R-squared from ``e(r2)``; NaN when not recorded.

properties.name: rsquared_adj
properties.docstring: Adjusted R-squared from ``e(r2_a)``; NaN when not recorded.

properties.name: stata_cov_params
properties.docstring:
``V`` in Stata's ``e(V)`` order (the same permutation as the names).

Raises
------
NotImplementedError
    For factor terms whose Stata layout has more rows than this result;
    see :attr:`stata_param_names`.

properties.name: stata_factor_terms
properties.docstring:
Factor terms whose Stata ``e(b)`` spelling cannot be reconstructed.

Stata expands an explicit factor into one coefficient per LEVEL plus an
explicit base row, so ``regress mpg weight i.foreign`` reports FOUR
entries -- ``weight``, ``0b.foreign``, ``1.foreign``, ``_cons`` -- with
the base recorded as 0 (``regress_auto_factor.json`` shows exactly that:
``b = [-0.00659, 0.0, -1.65003, 41.6797]``).

A plain binary variable is different: ``regress mpg weight foreign``
reports a single ``foreign`` row naming the level, which maps one-to-one
onto this package's ``foreign[T.Foreign]`` column. That case is fine and
is NOT reported here.

The discriminating question is therefore "is this an explicit factor
expansion, or a 0/1 variable?"  patsy spells both as ``[T.<level>]``, so
the check uses the source the caller wrote: a ``C(...)`` term is explicit,
a bare column whose values are all 0/1 is a dummy.

Returns
-------
list[str]
    Empty when every coefficient has an unambiguous Stata spelling.

Notes
-----
The discriminating question is what the CALLER wrote, not what patsy
produced: an explicit ``C(...)`` term is a factor expansion, while a bare
column is a variable Stata would render as one row -- even when the column
is a string that patsy had to code as a factor (the ``auto.dta``
``foreign`` column is ``"Domestic"``/``"Foreign"``, yet
``regress_auto.json`` reports a single ``foreign`` row).  So the check is
purely syntactic on the recorded parameter names.

properties.name: stata_param_names
properties.docstring:
Coefficient names as Stata reports them (``_cons`` last).

Raises
------
NotImplementedError
    When a factor term's Stata spelling is ambiguous -- Stata reports one
    row per level plus a zero base row, while this package has a single
    level column. See :attr:`stata_factor_terms`. Returning an invented
    name would be worse than refusing: it would look like a valid
    correspondence to Stata's ``e(b)`` row when none exists.

properties.name: stata_params
properties.docstring:
``b`` in Stata's ``e(b)`` order and spelling.

Raises
------
NotImplementedError
    For factor terms whose Stata spelling is ambiguous; see
    :attr:`stata_param_names`.

properties.name: zvalues
properties.docstring:
Normal statistic for :math:`H_0: \beta_j = 0`.

Stata reports this as ``z`` for models fitted by maximum likelihood.
It is numerically identical to :attr:`tvalues` (``params / bse``); the
alias exists so downstream code can branch on the inference
distribution without computing it again.

estat_ic.en: Information criteria for one fitted model. Prints AIC and BIC computed from the log-likelihood and the parameter count, following `estimates.ado:985-1002`. Unlike the `e(aic)` macro -- which several commands do not store at all, and which `regress` stores on a different scale -- this is the surface that matches what Stata's `estat ic` prints.
estat_ic.zh: 单个已拟合模型的信息准则。依据 `estimates.ado:985-1002`，由对数似然与参数个数计算 AIC 与 BIC 并打印。与 `e(aic)` 宏不同——若干命令根本不存该宏，而 `regress` 存的还在另一个尺度上——本函数才是与 Stata `estat ic` 输出一致的入口。
estat_ic.notes_en: `regress` stores no `e(aic)`; this function computes the criterion on demand, so it works there anyway.
estat_ic.notes_zh: `regress` 不存 `e(aic)`；本函数按需计算，因此在那里同样可用。

margins.en: Marginal effects and predictive margins. Supports the derivative forms Stata spells `dydx`, `eyex`, `dyex` and `eydx`, plus `at()` for fixing covariates and `over()` for group-wise margins. After a discrete-choice fit the derivative is taken on the response scale, which is what Stata's `margins` does -- the linear-index derivative would be a different quantity.
margins.zh: 边际效应与预测边际。支持 Stata 的 `dydx`、`eyex`、`dyex`、`eydx` 四种导数形式，以及 `at()` 固定协变量、`over()` 分组。拟合离散选择模型后在响应尺度上求导，这与 Stata `margins` 一致——线性指数上的导数会是另一个量。
margins.example: ws.margins(ws.Logit.from_formula('yb ~ x1 + x2', base).fit(), dydx='x1', at={'x2': 0.0})
margins.notes_en: Which prediction types `margins` may use is declared by the command itself in `e(marginsok)`/`e(marginsnotok)`; a type the command forbids is refused rather than silently computed.
margins.notes_zh: `margins` 可用哪些预测类型由命令自身通过 `e(marginsok)`/`e(marginsnotok)` 声明；被命令禁止的类型会被拒绝，而不是静默计算。

params.en: Point estimates as a `pandas.Series` indexed by `param_names`, in the column order the design matrix was built with. That order is patsy's, which puts the constant FIRST (`Intercept`), whereas Stata's `e(b)` puts `_cons` LAST; the two vectors hold the same numbers in a different order. Use `stata_params` when the comparison is against Stata's `e(b)`.
params.zh: 点估计值，以 `param_names` 为索引的 `pandas.Series`，顺序与构建设计矩阵时的列序一致。该顺序是 patsy 的顺序，常数项排在最前（`Intercept`），而 Stata 的 `e(b)` 把 `_cons` 排在最后；两个向量数值相同但顺序不同。要与 Stata 的 `e(b)` 对比时请用 `stata_params`。
params.example:
r = ws.OLS.from_formula('y ~ x1 + x2', base).fit()
r.params

bse.en: Standard errors, the square roots of the diagonal of the covariance matrix that `cov_type` selected. They are computed once at construction from `cov`, so a caller who changes the covariance afterwards does not change `bse`.
bse.zh: 标准误，即 `cov_type` 所选协方差矩阵对角线的平方根。它在构造时由 `cov` 一次算出，因此之后改动协方差不会改变 `bse`。
bse.example:
r = ws.OLS.from_formula('y ~ x1 + x2', base).fit()
r.bse

pvalues.stata: regress -- the `P>|t|` column; logit -- the `P>|z|` column
pvalues.en: Two-sided p-values for the null that each coefficient is zero. The reference distribution follows `dist`: Student t with `df_resid` degrees of freedom when `dist` is `"t"`, the standard normal when it is `"z"`. A model whose `df_resid` is `G - 1` from a clustered VCE therefore uses that count, not `nobs - k`.
pvalues.zh: 各系数为零这一原假设的双侧 p 值。参照分布由 `dist` 决定：`dist` 为 `"t"` 时用自由度为 `df_resid` 的 Student t 分布，为 `"z"` 时用标准正态分布。因此聚类 VCE 下 `df_resid` 为 `G - 1` 的模型用的是该计数，而不是 `nobs - k`。
pvalues.example:
r = ws.OLS.from_formula('y ~ x1 + x2', base).fit()
r.pvalues

tvalues.en: The coefficient divided by its standard error, always named `tvalues` even for a z-based model. It is the test statistic, not a t statistic as such: for a logit fit the same numbers are the z statistics Stata prints. `zvalues` is the same object under the name the distribution calls for.
tvalues.zh: 系数除以其标准误，即便对基于 z 的模型也始终命名为 `tvalues`。它是检验统计量，而非严格意义上的 t 统计量：对 logit 拟合，这些数字就是 Stata 打印的 z 值。`zvalues` 是同一对象，只是用了分布所对应的名字。
tvalues.example:
r = ws.OLS.from_formula('y ~ x1 + x2', base).fit()
r.tvalues

zvalues.en: The normal statistic for the null that a coefficient is zero. It is numerically identical to `tvalues` -- both are `params / bse` -- and is exposed under this name so downstream code can branch on the inference distribution without recomputing it. It is an alias, not an independent calculation, so the Series it returns still carries the name `tvalues`.
zvalues.zh: 系数为零这一原假设的正态统计量。它与 `tvalues` 在数值上完全相同（两者都是 `params / bse`），之所以以这个名字暴露，是为了让下游代码能按推断分布分支而无需重算。它是别名而非独立计算，因此返回的 Series 仍带有 `tvalues` 这个名字。
zvalues.example:
r = ws.Logit.from_formula('yb ~ x1 + x2', base).fit()
r.zvalues

fvalue.en: The model's joint F statistic, read from `e(F)`; NaN when the command does not store it. Likelihood-based commands report a chi-square model test instead, stored as `e(chi2)`, so `fvalue` is NaN after a logit or Poisson fit -- that is the correct absence, not a missing calculation.
fvalue.zh: 模型的联合 F 统计量，取自 `e(F)`；命令不存该宏时为 NaN。基于似然的命令改报卡方模型检验，存为 `e(chi2)`，因此 logit 或 Poisson 拟合后 `fvalue` 是 NaN——这是正确的“不存在”，而非漏算。
fvalue.example:
r = ws.OLS.from_formula('y ~ x1 + x2', base).fit()
r.fvalue

llf.en: The maximised log-likelihood, read from `e(ll)`; NaN when the command does not record it. It is the number `estat ic` and `lrtest` build their statistics from, so a fit that reports NaN here cannot support either of them.
llf.zh: 最大化对数似然，取自 `e(ll)`；命令不记录该宏时为 NaN。`estat ic` 与 `lrtest` 的统计量都由这个数构成，因此此处报 NaN 的拟合无法支撑这两者。
llf.example:
r = ws.OLS.from_formula('y ~ x1 + x2', base).fit()
r.llf

aic.stata: e(aic) -- note that `estat ic` is the surface that matches Stata's printed table
aic.en: AIC read from `e(aic)`; NaN when the command does not record it. For `regress` this is NOT the number `estat ic` prints: `regress` stores no AIC at all, and the value exposed here is on the Gaussian-deviance scale, `N log(rss/N) + 2k`, which is a different quantity from the likelihood-scale `-2 logL + 2k`. For commands that do store `e(aic)` the two agree.
aic.zh: 取自 `e(aic)` 的 AIC；命令不记录该宏时为 NaN。对 `regress` 而言这不是 `estat ic` 打印的那个数：`regress` 根本不存 AIC，此处暴露的值在正态偏差尺度上，即 `N log(rss/N) + 2k`，与似然尺度的 `-2 logL + 2k` 是不同的量。对确实存 `e(aic)` 的命令，两者一致。
aic.example:
r = ws.OLS.from_formula('y ~ x1 + x2', base).fit()
(r.aic, ws.estat_ic(r).aic)
aic.notes_en: Do not compare `result.aic` against `estat ic` output for a `regress` fit; they are on different scales. `e(_aic_is_stata)` records which sense applies, and the summary table prints AIC only when that flag says the value is Stata's.
aic.notes_zh: 不要把 `result.aic` 与 `regress` 拟合的 `estat ic` 输出相比；两者尺度不同。`e(_aic_is_stata)` 记录适用的是哪一种含义，摘要表仅在该标志表明该值即 Stata 的值时才打印 AIC。

bic.stata: e(bic) -- with the same caveat as `aic`
bic.en: BIC read from `e(bic)`; NaN when the command does not record it. The same scale caveat as `aic` applies: after `regress` the stored value is the Gaussian-deviance `N log(rss/N) + k log(N)`, not the likelihood-scale criterion `estat ic` prints.
bic.zh: 取自 `e(bic)` 的 BIC；命令不记录该宏时为 NaN。`aic` 的尺度注意事项同样适用：`regress` 之后存的值是正态偏差形式 `N log(rss/N) + k log(N)`，而非 `estat ic` 打印的似然尺度准则。
bic.example:
r = ws.OLS.from_formula('y ~ x1 + x2', base).fit()
(r.bic, ws.estat_ic(r).bic)

nobs.en: The number of ROWS in the estimation sample, as an integer. It is deliberately not `e(N)` under frequency weights: with `fweight` the rows are replication counts, so `e(N)` becomes `sum(w)` while `nobs` stays the row count. Use `result.e['N']` for the effective sample size.
nobs.zh: 估计样本的行数，为整数。在频数权重下它刻意不等于 `e(N)`：使用 `fweight` 时行是重复计数，因此 `e(N)` 变为 `sum(w)`，而 `nobs` 仍是行数。有效样本量请用 `result.e['N']`。
nobs.example:
r = ws.OLS.from_formula('y ~ x1 + x2', base).fit()
(r.nobs, r.e['N'])

df_model.en: Model degrees of freedom, i.e. the number of restrictions the model test imposes: the regressors excluding the constant. It is read from `e(df_m)`, so for a one-regressor model it is 1, not 2, even though the coefficient vector has two entries.
df_model.zh: 模型自由度，即模型检验施加的约束个数：不含常数项的回归元个数。它取自 `e(df_m)`，因此单回归元模型的值为 1 而非 2，尽管系数向量有两个元素。
df_model.example:
r = ws.OLS.from_formula('y ~ x1 + x2', base).fit()
r.df_model

df_resid.en: The denominator degrees of freedom the reference distribution uses. It is NOT always `nobs - k`: for a clustered VCE it is `G - 1`, the number of clusters minus one. This property returns the value the estimator computed at fit time; `e(df_r)` is a separate matter, because that macro is only present for non-z models (or when an estimator such as `tobit` or `xtivreg` supplied it explicitly), so a logit fit has a `df_resid` here and no `e(df_r)`.
df_resid.zh: 参照分布使用的分母自由度。它并不总是 `nobs - k`：聚类 VCE 下为 `G - 1`，即聚类数减一。本属性返回估计器在拟合时算出的值；`e(df_r)` 是另一回事，因为该宏只对非 z 模型存在（或由 `tobit`、`xtivreg` 等估计器显式提供），因此 logit 拟合在这里有 `df_resid`，却没有 `e(df_r)`。
df_resid.example:
r = ws.OLS.from_formula('y ~ x1', base).fit(cov_type='cluster', cov_kwds={'groups': base['firm']})
(r.df_resid, r.cov_type)

dist.stata: (no Stata equivalent -- Stata picks t or z per command and stores it in e() indirectly)
dist.en: Which reference distribution inference uses: `"t"` for t statistics and t confidence intervals, `"z"` for normal tests. It is decided by the estimator, not by the caller, and it is what `pvalues` and `conf_int` branch on. A linear fit reports `t`; logit, probit and the count models report `z`.
dist.zh: 推断所使用的参照分布：`"t"` 表示 t 统计量与 t 置信区间，`"z"` 表示正态检验。它由估计器而非调用者决定，`pvalues` 与 `conf_int` 正是据此分支。线性拟合报 `t`；logit、probit 与计数模型报 `z`。
dist.example:
r = ws.Logit.from_formula('yb ~ x1 + x2', base).fit()
r.dist

model_name.en: The Stata command name of the estimator that produced the result -- `regress`, `logit`, `reghdfe` and so on -- which is also the label the summary prints. When the estimator did not record `e(cmd)`, this value is used to synthesise it, so `result.e['cmd']` is always available even though Stata always stores it.
model_name.zh: 产生该结果的估计器对应的 Stata 命令名——`regress`、`logit`、`reghdfe` 等——它同时也是摘要打印的标签。估计器未记录 `e(cmd)` 时，用该值合成，因此 `result.e['cmd']` 总是可用，尽管 Stata 本身总是会存它。
model_name.example:
r = ws.OLS.from_formula('y ~ x1 + x2', base).fit()
r.model_name

cov_type.stata: e(vce) / e(vcetype) -- the `Covariance Type` line of the summary
cov_type.en: Label of the covariance estimator that was used, kept for display and auditing: `nonrobust` by default, `HC1` for heteroskedasticity-robust, `cluster` for clustered. It is a recorded label, not a switch; changing it after the fact changes nothing, because the matrix itself was built at fit time.
cov_type.zh: 所用协方差估计器的标签，用于展示与审计：默认 `nonrobust`，异方差稳健为 `HC1`，聚类为 `cluster`。它是记录下来的标签而非开关，事后修改不会改变任何东西，因为矩阵本身在拟合时已构建完成。
cov_type.example:
r = ws.OLS.from_formula('y ~ x1 + x2', base).fit(cov_type='HC1')
r.cov_type

cov.en: The coefficient covariance matrix as a `k x k` numpy array, already carrying every small-sample correction that was requested. It is the same object `cov_params()` returns; `cov_params()` exists only so statsmodels-compatible code that calls a method finds one. Order follows `param_names`, so it is patsy's order, not Stata's `e(V)` order.
cov.zh: 系数协方差矩阵，为 `k x k` 的 numpy 数组，已包含所请求的全部小样本修正。它与 `cov_params()` 返回的是同一对象；`cov_params()` 的存在只是为了满足按方法调用的 statsmodels 兼容代码。顺序遵循 `param_names`，即 patsy 顺序，而非 Stata 的 `e(V)` 顺序。
cov.example:
r = ws.OLS.from_formula('y ~ x1 + x2', base).fit()
np.round(r.cov, 4)

e.en: The Stata `e()` macros as a dictionary-like object with BOTH item and attribute access. Item access keeps normal mapping semantics and raises `KeyError` for a macro the command did not store; attribute access is deliberately forgiving and returns `None` instead. The key set DIFFERS PER COMMAND -- assuming uniformity is exactly how invented keys get added to a manual: `regress` stores no `aic` on the `estat ic` scale and `tobit` stores no `aic` at all.
e.zh: 以字典式对象提供的 Stata `e()` 宏，同时支持下标与属性访问。下标访问保持普通映射语义，命令未存的宏会抛 `KeyError`；属性访问则刻意宽容，返回 `None`。键集逐命令不同——假定它统一，正是手册里凭空多出键的原因：`regress` 在 `estat ic` 尺度上不存 `aic`，`tobit` 则根本不存 `aic`。
e.example:
r = ws.OLS.from_formula('y ~ x1 + x2', base).fit()
sorted(r.e)
e.notes_en: Two macros are synthesised because every command documents them: `e(depvar)` from the response name and `e(cmd)` from `model_name`. `e(cmdline)` is deliberately NOT synthesised -- it records the command as typed, options included, and this package has no such string, so inventing one would fabricate a value.
e.notes_zh: 有两个宏是合成出来的，因为每条命令都记录它们：`e(depvar)` 取自响应变量名，`e(cmd)` 取自 `model_name`。`e(cmdline)` 刻意不合成——它记录的是用户键入的原样命令（含选项），本包没有该字符串，编造一个即为伪造值。

fittedvalues.en: The fitted values on the estimation sample, a numpy array of length `nobs` in row order. For weighted fits these are the predictions of the weighted least-squares problem, not weighted fitted values. `predict(kind='xb')` recomputes the same quantity from the retained design matrix, which is what to use for out-of-sample data.
fittedvalues.zh: 估计样本上的拟合值，长度为 `nobs`、按行序排列的 numpy 数组。加权拟合时它们是加权最小二乘问题的预测值，而非加权后的拟合值。`predict(kind='xb')` 会从保留下来的设计矩阵重算同一个量，样本外数据应改用该入口。
fittedvalues.example:
r = ws.OLS.from_formula('y ~ x1 + x2', base).fit()
r.fittedvalues[:5]

resid.en: Residuals on the estimation sample, `y - fittedvalues`, a numpy array of length `nobs`. They are raw residuals, not standardised or studentised ones, and for weighted fits they are the raw deviations rather than the weighted residuals.
resid.zh: 估计样本上的残差，即 `y - fittedvalues`，长度为 `nobs` 的 numpy 数组。它们是原始残差，而非标准化或学生化残差；加权拟合时它们是原始离差，而非加权残差。
resid.example:
r = ws.OLS.from_formula('y ~ x1 + x2', base).fit()
r.resid[:5]

param_names.stata: row names of e(b) -- but in patsy spelling and order
param_names.en: The coefficient names, in coefficient order, as a list of strings. The spelling is patsy's: `Intercept` first, factor levels as `foreign[T.Foreign]`, interactions with `:`. Stata spells these `_cons` last, `foreign` for a bare dummy, and `#` for interactions; `stata_param_names` performs that translation.
param_names.zh: 系数名，按系数顺序排列的字符串列表。拼写是 patsy 的：`Intercept` 在前，因子水平写作 `foreign[T.Foreign]`，交互项用 `:`。Stata 则把 `_cons` 排在最后、裸哑变量写作 `foreign`、交互项用 `#`；`stata_param_names` 负责该转换。
param_names.example:
r = ws.OLS.from_formula('y ~ x1 + x2', base).fit()
r.param_names

rsquared.en: R-squared read from `e(r2)`; NaN when the command does not record it. This exists for the OLS family; the maximum-likelihood families store a pseudo R-squared in `e(r2_p)` instead and leave this NaN, so a NaN here means "this model has no R-squared", not a failed computation. Read `e['r2_p']` for logit, probit and the count models.
rsquared.zh: 取自 `e(r2)` 的 R²；命令不记录该宏时为 NaN。它属于 OLS 一族；极大似然族改在 `e(r2_p)` 中存伪 R²，此处留作 NaN，因此这里的 NaN 表示“该模型没有 R²”，而非计算失败。logit、probit 与计数模型请读 `e['r2_p']`。
rsquared.example:
ols = ws.OLS.from_formula('y ~ x1 + x2', base).fit()
lg = ws.Logit.from_formula('yb ~ x1 + x2', base).fit()
((ols.rsquared, lg.rsquared), lg.e['r2_p'])

rsquared_adj.en: Adjusted R-squared read from `e(r2_a)`; NaN when the command does not record it. Like `rsquared` it belongs to the linear family, and the degrees-of-freedom adjustment uses the effective sample size, so a frequency-weighted fit corrects by `sum(w)` rather than by the row count.
rsquared_adj.zh: 取自 `e(r2_a)` 的调整 R²；命令不记录该宏时为 NaN。与 `rsquared` 一样它属于线性族，其自由度修正使用有效样本量，因此频数加权拟合按 `sum(w)` 而非行数修正。
rsquared_adj.example:
r = ws.OLS.from_formula('y ~ x1 + x2', base).fit()
r.rsquared_adj

stata_param_names.stata: the row names of e(b) as Stata spells and orders them
stata_param_names.en: Coefficient names in Stata's `e(b)` order and spelling: regressors first, then `_cons` LAST, then auxiliary parameters such as `cut1` or `lnalpha`. `Intercept` becomes `_cons`, a bare factor column takes the variable name without the level, `:` becomes `#`, and a leading `/` is dropped. Raises `NotImplementedError` for an explicit `C(...)` factor, where Stata has one row per level plus a zero base row and no one-to-one mapping exists.
stata_param_names.zh: 按 Stata 的 `e(b)` 顺序与拼写给出的系数名：先是回归元，然后 `_cons` 在最后，最后是 `cut1` 或 `lnalpha` 等辅助参数。`Intercept` 变为 `_cons`，裸因子列取变量名而省略水平，`:` 变 `#`，前导 `/` 被去掉。对显式 `C(...)` 因子会抛 `NotImplementedError`，因为 Stata 为每个水平给一行再加一行零基准，不存在一一映射。
stata_param_names.example:
r = ws.OLS.from_formula('y ~ x1 + x2', base).fit()
(r.param_names, r.stata_param_names)

stata_params.en: The coefficient vector permuted into Stata's `e(b)` order and spelling: `_cons` last instead of first, factor and interaction names rewritten. It is a property, not a method -- write `r.stata_params`, not `r.stata_params()`. The numbers are identical to `params`, only the order and the labels differ, and this is the view to compare against a Stata fixture.
stata_params.zh: 重排为 Stata `e(b)` 顺序与拼写的系数向量：`_cons` 移到末尾而非开头，因子与交互项名称重写。它是属性而非方法——写 `r.stata_params`，不要写 `r.stata_params()`。数值与 `params` 完全相同，只是顺序与标签不同，与 Stata fixture 对比时应用此视图。
stata_params.example:
r = ws.OLS.from_formula('y ~ x1 + x2', base).fit()
r.stata_params

stata_cov_params.en: The covariance matrix permuted by the same ordering as `stata_params`, as a numpy array. It surfaces the same refusal as the names for an ambiguous factor term, so a caller cannot receive a matrix whose rows silently disagree with Stata's. Use this rather than `cov` when the comparison target is Stata's `e(V)`.
stata_cov_params.zh: 按与 `stata_params` 相同的顺序重排后的协方差矩阵，为 numpy 数组。对含义不明确的因子项，它抛出与名称访问相同的拒绝，因此调用者不会拿到一个行序与 Stata 静默不一致的矩阵。比较对象是 Stata 的 `e(V)` 时请用它而非 `cov`。
stata_cov_params.example:
r = ws.OLS.from_formula('y ~ x1 + x2', base).fit()
np.round(r.stata_cov_params, 4)

stata_factor_terms.stata: i.<var> -- the explicit factor expansion in a varlist
stata_factor_terms.en: The factor terms whose Stata `e(b)` spelling cannot be reconstructed, as a sorted list; empty when every coefficient has an unambiguous Stata spelling. Stata expands an explicit `i.foreign` into one row per level plus an explicit zero base row (`0b.foreign`), while this package has a single level column, so there is no one-to-one mapping. A bare binary column is NOT reported here, because Stata names its single row after the variable.
stata_factor_terms.zh: 无法重建其 Stata `e(b)` 拼写的因子项，为排序后的列表；当每个系数都有明确的 Stata 拼写时为空。Stata 把显式 `i.foreign` 展开为每个水平一行再加一行显式零基准（`0b.foreign`），而本包只有一个水平列，故不存在一一映射。裸二元列不会出现在此，因为 Stata 用变量名为其单独一行命名。
stata_factor_terms.example:
r = ws.OLS.from_formula('y ~ x1 + C(yb)', base).fit()
r.stata_factor_terms
stata_factor_terms.notes_en: Non-empty here means `stata_param_names`, `stata_params` and `stata_cov_params` all raise `NotImplementedError` on this result; compare with `params`/`bse`, or encode the factor as dummies and refit.
stata_factor_terms.notes_zh: 此处非空意味着该结果上的 `stata_param_names`、`stata_params` 与 `stata_cov_params` 都会抛 `NotImplementedError`；请改用 `params`/`bse` 对比，或把因子编码为哑变量后重新拟合。

converged.en: Whether the optimizer reported convergence, read from `e(converged)`. An ABSENT macro is reported as `True` rather than `False`, because it means the estimator runs no iterative optimizer at all -- a closed-form fit has nothing to fail to converge. So `True` has two senses here: "converged" for an ML fit and "not applicable" for OLS.
converged.zh: 优化器是否报告收敛，取自 `e(converged)`。该宏缺失时报 `True` 而非 `False`：缺失意味着估计器根本不跑迭代优化，闭式解没有“收敛失败”可言。因此 `True` 在此有两种含义：对 ML 拟合是“已收敛”，对 OLS 是“不适用”。
converged.example:
r = ws.Logit.from_formula('yb ~ x1 + x2', base).fit()
(r.converged, r.iterations, r.grad_norm)
